subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1983-84 (NO. 2) MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext:
that Bill C-151, an Act to provide supplementary borrowing authority, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs.
He said: Mr. Speaker, in beginning my comments on Bill C-151,1 would like to draw to the attention of Hon. Members the remarks of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) on October 27, 1982 when as the Minister of Finance he presented his comments on an economic plan in Parliament. I quote from his comments:
I have also made it clear by the estimates I have presented that further borrowing authority will be required before the end of this fiscal year. In the budget I intend to present early in 1983, I will review again the fiscal situation for the current fiscal year, set out estimates for 1983-84 and future fiscal years, and then seek additional borrowing authority as required.
[DOT]	(1110)
The Minister of Finance in his speech on supplementary borrowing authority of February 17, 1983 made reference as well to his intention to seek authority as is sought in Bill C-151 by these words:
I intend to introduce a Bill covering all of the borrowing authority needed for fiscal year 1983-84 after providing Parliament with the necessary information in my budget.
During debate on borrowing authority at the time the Minister made that speech, Members opposite insisted that they were not seeking to interfere with Government operations and they were not necessarily challenging the valuable social assistance programs that are supported by this borrowing authority. It was argued that they were willing to deal with borrowing authority if only they had adequate financial information. For example, on February 17, 1983 the Hon. Member for Vancouver Centre (Miss Carney) stated that her Party:
-would be much more willing to debate and pass this Bill if we knew what the money was needed for-
The Member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn), who is in the House today, also indicated, both in Committee and in
the House of Commons, that he would be willing to pass the legislation quickly if the Minister would give him a reasonable explanation of the economic position of the country with respect to the current fiscal year. He said that in the House on March 22 of this year.
The budget has been presented, Mr. Speaker. It does contain current and fiscal year projections. The budget contains the Government's economic forecast and its assumptions about the country's likely economic performance. We have, in effect, laid our cards on the table and provided the information which is the basis for the borrowing authority sought in Bill C-151. As Members opposite have indicated, they may quarrel with any or all aspects of the budget or its background information, but certainly they cannot argue that we have not presented, as comprehensively as we are able to, the basis for the request for speedy consideration of the Bill before the House, Mr. Speaker.
The Financial Administration Act stipulates that, except when Section 39 is used, statutory borrowing authority must be obtained from Parliament in order for the Government to increase its debt and to have additional authority for borrowing. Under Part IV Section 36 of the Act is the legislative basis for the request before us today. It reads:
No money shall be borrowed or security issued by or on behalf of Her Majesty without the authority of Parliament.
This refers to new money only, as under Section 38 of the Act there is a continuing authority to borrow funds to repay maturing debts. Consequently, in order for the Government to borrow money to meet its financial requirements, statutory borrowing authority must be obtained from Parliament. Section 39 does provide for the Governor in Council to authorize the borrowing of money when it appears that funds will not be sufficient to meet disbursements from the Consolidated Revenue Fund. This legislation is designed for short-term loans under limited terms to maturity not exceeding six months.
I have indicated the legislative basis of the legislation for which approval is sought today. I have indicated that the material which is the financial basis and foundation of that legislation is before us. We are now seeking speedy consideration of this legislation by the Opposition.
In so far as the budget is concerned, Hon. Members will know that it contains a large number of new initiatives to support and encourage economic recovery, to create jobs and to position the economy to take full advantage of the economic expansion phase that is developing in the world economies and reflected in the Canadian economy.

May 5, 1983
Borrowing Authority
S)
The $4.8 billion program of private investment incentives and public spending is the main centrepiece of the budget strategy. We believe it will lead to the creation of good, rewarding jobs for Canadians right across Canada and that it will improve the economic basis on which our growth potential depends so much. Plans for federal capital projects worth half of that amount, that is $2.4 billion, are being finalized. As Hon. Members know, they will be put on a fast track in order to ensure that their contribution to the economic recovery comes quickly, within weeks.
Additional tax incentives through the business sector comprise the balance of the $2.4 billion, and this provision has received almost unanimously favourable comment across the country in the days since the budget. We believe this centrepiece, the $2.4 billion of accelerated and new funding, will contribute greatly to economic recovery.
The Special Recovery Program will go some distance in stimulating job creation in Canada, not only immediately under the capital works projects that we have set for the months and years ahead, but as well by virtue of the building blocks that the tax incentives, which are permanent changes to the Income Tax Act, will achieve.
The Government is doing more toward this end of creating jobs. The housing sector will benefit, and benefit greatly, from the measures in the budget and construction-related employment will continue to expand rapidly. The specific measures which will provide stimulus in this sector include modifications to the Registered Home Ownership Savings Plan, extension of the Canada Home Ownership Stimulation Plan and the Canadian Home Renovation Plan, as well as additional allocations for the Residential Rehabilitation Assistance Plan, for both Indian and social housing.
Furthermore, the Government is providing major additional support to employment through direct job creation measures. More funds have been allocated for the New Employment Expansion and Development Plan for local employment initiatives and for special youth job creation programs of several kinds, including the Summer Canada Program, Katimavik, the new defence Extended Youth Training and Employment Program and youth wage subsidy and internship programs. All of these allocations in the budget to which I have referred bring the total federal amount to be spent on direct job creation in 1983-84 to $1.5 billion, a figure which is impressive both on its own and in comparison to previous spending of the Government.
On the other hand, as indicated in the budget revenue growth is likely to remain relatively weak this year and the budgetary deficit is expected to be $31.3 billion. The net source of funds provided by non-budgetary transactions is projected to be somewhat larger for 1983-84 than it was in 1982-83, due in large part to the increase in Unemployment Insurance premiums that took effect on January 1, 1983. Thus estimated financial requirements, excluding foreign exchange transactions, are forecast to be $26.6 billion this fiscal year.
Passage of the present borrowing authority Bill, Bill C-151, of which we are speaking today, will ensure the Government is
in a position to implement the important measures in the budget and to meet the projected requirements for funds as identified in that plan for economic recovery.
The request for borrowing authority in 1983-84 is based on the financial requirements that I have mentioned, plus a reserve for contingencies. As we already have $14 billion in borrowing authority for the current fiscal year, we are seeking an additional $12.7 billion, to provide us with a total of $26.7 billion borrowing authority for the current year, an amount equivalent to the financial requirements, plus an amount for contingencies.
For purposes of clarity, Mr. Speaker, I would for the benefit of Hon. Members like to set out the history of the borrowing authority numbers in more detail. Part II of Bill C-143 passed last March provided interim borrowing authority of $14 billion for 1983-84. In addition, Part I of Bill C-143 conferred $5 billion of borrowing authority on the Government for use in the years 1982-83, of which an unused amount in excess of $2 billion was to expire on March 31, 1983. As it turned out-and I will provide the House with details later on-there was $2 billion of unused authority available to be carried forward into 1983-84.
Clause 2(1) of the Bill currently before the House seeks additional borrowing authority for fiscal 1983-84 of $14.7 billion. Clause 2(2) of Bill C-151 provides that any unused portion of this amount, to the extent that it exceeds $2 billion, will be cancelled on March 31, 1984. Thus passage of the current Bill, along with the borrowing authority provided in Bill C-143, will provide a total of $26.7 billion in new borrowing authority for 1983-84, plus a non-lapsing contigency of $4 billion.
There are two fundamental reasons, Mr. Speaker, for the non-lapsing contingency. They were the reasons, Mr. Speaker, which had prompted Parliament to put such a contingency in borrowing authorities previously, and they were borrowing authorities not only of this Government, but under the regime of Hon. Members opposite when they formed the Government as well. First, there is a need to have an amount in place to accommodate exchange market pressures and the effect they have on the level of official exchange reserves. Second, it is to enable the Government to continue with its regular debt program when the House is not in session.
In the foreign exchange market, when the Canadian dollar is firm the exchange fund account accumulates American dollars, and in order to finance this increase in official reserves, Canadian dollars must either be taken from cash balances or borrowed and charged against the borrowing authority.
On the other hand, when the dollar is weak the U.S. dollar reserves fall and these balances must be supplemented by drawing on the two standby credit facilities which the Government has with both the Canadian and international banks, or
May 5, 1983

by other types of foreign borrowings. Any of these borrowings must be charged against the borrowing authority. This has been the practice of the Government for many years. It was the practice, as I said, which was carried on by Hon. Members opposite when they formed the Government.
Events which took place in May and June, 1982 are probably the best example to illustrate the type of situation which I have called upon just now. In that period the dollar was under pressure and nearly $3.5 billion of borrowing authority was used for foreign borrowing. And for all of 1982-83 foreign exchange operations added $1.5 billion to the financial requirements.
It is in case of any such repeated circumstances, Mr. Speaker, that we have asked for the contingency. As I say, such contingency has been granted by Parliament on all previous requests made heretofore. The request for a non-lapsing contingency amount, therefore, is not new.
I would like to turn, Mr. Speaker, to an explanation of how the borrowing authority situation stood at the end of 1982-83. Including the $5 billion borrowing authority provided by Bill C-143, the total amount of authority granted for 1982-83 was about $26.1 billion. Approximately $23.1 billion of this amount was used; $9.7 billion through the issue of Treasury bills, $4.9 billion through the issue of bonds, and $7.6 billion net Canada Saving Bonds sales. Foreign borrowing added a further $.9 billion to the use of borrowing authority. The foreign borrowing represented U.S. $750 million borrowed in the Eurobond market last June, and a partial redemption of Deutschemark maturity early last year. Thus there was approximately $3 billion unused of which $2 billion, as I indicated, was carried forward, and about $1 billion was cancelled on March 31, 1983.
I mentioned at the outset, Mr. Speaker, that Section 39 of the Financial Administration Act can be used in special circumstances. I would like to make reference to the actual amount of Treasury bills that were used by the Government under Section 39. Hon. Members will recall that in mid-February virtually all of the borrowing authority authorized for 1982-83 had been used. By early March it became apparent that Bill C-143 would not be passed for several weeks. In fact, we know that Royal Assent was not received until March 30.
Projected Financial requirements over the March to June period were extremely large, and in order to continue with a regular debt program that would satisfy these requirements it was decided to make use of the temporary powers granted by Section 39 of the Financial Administration Act. Permission was sought from Cabinet to use Section 39 to authorize a total of $2.3 billion of net new Treasury bill issues over the March 11-31 period. However, due to Canada Savings Bond redemptions occurring during that period which had the effect of increasing the authority, and since new authority was conferred in time to authorize the March 31 issue of Treasury bills, total usage of Section 39 amounted to approximately

$1.4 billion. This amount was in any event charged to the new authority under Bill C-143.
I would like to refer to the final clause in Bill C-151, Mr. Speaker, which has recently been a standard clause. Clause 2.3 refers to the ability of the Government to borrow and repay loans in foreign currency and has been included in the last six Borrowing Authority Acts. Over the years Canada has borrowed and repaid funds in a number of currencies. In recent years, however, this Clause has been added to confirm Canada's right to borrow in foreign currencies.
Bill C-96, which received first reading in the House in March, 1982, proposes a number of amendments to the Financial Administration Act, including a general amendment clarifying the Government's ability to borrow and repay in foreign currencies. Once this amendment has been passed, there will no longer be any need to have the specific request included in the borrowing legislation, such as Bill C-151 before the House today.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I began my comments by pointing out that the Minister of Finance had, in the fall of last year, in his first official statement to the House as Minister of Finance, indicated his intention to seek the authority we are today asking for. He again made reference to his intention to seek the authority once a fiscal and economic plan had been placed before Parliament and we have concluded debate on that budget. The vote recently concluded the initial debate on that exercise.
In the request of the Government for interim borrowing authority, we took the opportunity to remind Hon. Members that the last occasion prior to today when borrowing authority was requested was for borrowing authority pending the production of the budget and the financial material in the budget, although the Estimates had themselves been presented earlier. Therefore, today Bill C-151 is a follow-through of the Minister's intention signalled in October of last year to seek the support of Hon. Members to provide the wherewithal to carry out the economic program which is so important to this country at this time, especially those features of the Government's plan identified in the budget as the Special Recovery Program, at the same time maintaining the Government's support of its social net and safety provisions which have been and are so important to Canadians less fortunate than others who have, for example, needed the support of the Unemployment Insurance Fund. The request today is to continue the Government's new initiative in its economic plan and to continue its social commitment to Canadians who need that kind of support at this time.
The legislation, I understand, would go to committee for detailed examination. Hopefully, the consideration at second reading, the deliberation by committee, the return to the House and the proceeding with the legislation to ensure support for economic recovery, which has been well received

May 5, 1983
Borrowing Authority
by Canadians right across this country, would continue in a manner which illustrates the commitment of Parliament toward supporting the recovery which is very apparent.

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1983-84 (NO. 2) MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext:
Yes, Mr. Speaker. I have indicated that the practice of the Government in preceding requests for borrowing authority in Bills has always been to ask for non-lapsing contingencies. It is the Government's best estimate that a prudent amount to be held for contingencies would be the additional $4 billion.
We requested that for two reasons which I made evident. The first is the need to protect the Government's flexibility in foreign exchange markets. I gave an example as to how the Government had to intervene last year to the extent of $1.9 billion in a rapidly fluctuating foreign exchange period. The Government has no assurance, but that situation might occur or might not occur again. The point is that the Government needs that flexibility to protect the orderly movement of the Canadian dollar.
Second, the Government is requesting the contingency because it does not want to be in the position in which it found itself in having to rely on Section 39, an extraordinary measure to which the Government had to resort for the first time this year. In order not to be put into that position, the Government has requested the $4 billion. We are motivated in requesting the $4 billion because it is our feeling that when we had to rely on Section 39, it did conceivably have some impact on the markets and on interest rates in Canada. When interest rates rose, we felt that could have reflected the tardiness involving the last interim borrowing authority process in the House. Therefore, it is our best guess that the $4 billion is a prudent request for contingency.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank the Minister for that clarification. In opening debate on Bill C-151, an Act to provide supplementary borrowing authority, I want to stress that this Government is either callous or careless. It is callous because it is asking Parliament to approve a Bill for $4 billion more than it needs according to its own fiscal requirements as set out in the budget. It is callous because that padded borrowing must be added to the increasing debt which must be paid for, in the final analysis, by our children.
It is careless because padding the deficit by that amount of money, $4 billion, indicates that the Government is indeed acknowledging that its sloppy and slipshod financial projections are continually changing. It is also careless because it is all too clear that by padding the borrowing Bill and padding the deficit forecast, the Government is providing itself with an election slush fund to be borrowed and spent before Canadian voters turf the Liberals out.
This Government has come before Parliament seven times this session to ask it for more borrowing authority. In the fiscal year 1982-83 alone, the Government came hat in hand to Parliament for authority to borrow more money on four separate occasions. Just a few weeks ago we approved the largest borrowing Bill in our parliamentary history, Bill C-143.
The Government still has $16 billion of that borrowing authority left. Since its financial projections as stated in the budget and confirmed by the Minister are for $26.7 billion in the current fiscal year, it requires only $10.7 billion for the balance of the year. Further, the Minister himself has told us that the Government requires $2 billion in cash balances. Yet as of this week he has almost $6 billion-plus on hand. In fact, when one subtracts the surplus $3 billion cash in hand from his financial requirements, the Government requires only $7.7 billion in additional borrowing authority to meet the fiscal proposals set out in the April budget.
We have already seen how a careless Finance Minister can add $200 million worth of debt to cover up his inadvertent
Borrowing Authority
budget leak. We now see how the same Minister can pad billions of dollars to the borrowing authority and to the public debt.
Further, by returning to Parliament so soon after his last borrowing Bill, the Minister is showing his contempt for Parliament. He wants this Bill approved now so that he can avoid parliamentary scrutiny of his spending plans for the balance of the fiscal year which will end close to an election. He wants to spend his borrowed funds without the inconvenience of explaining to Parliament and the country how he means to use them. He will use these borrowed funds to establish his election goody bag. That is a shameless abuse of the institution of Parliament and it is one reason why we oppose this Bill.
The Government must be accountable to Parliament and Parliament must be accountable to the people. The Government cannot account for the billions of dollars requested in this Bill which is surplus to its cash reserves, its existing borrowing powers and its spending plans as set out in the budget.
We must remember that this is the same Government that took four runs at estimating last year's deficit, tripling it in the process, before giving up and saying that it would come in "somewhere" between its third and fourth estimates. Who suffers? Not just Parliament or Canadians who are required to foot this Bill and who will be paying an additional $5.7 billion in tax increases over the next four years. The real victims of this Government's dishonest approach will be our youth, who will be paying for years to come. That will be their legacy from the Liberal Party.
Who are the winners and who will benefit, at least in the short term, from this Liberal largesse? The Government has a long history of paying off its supporters and rewarding its friends. The Government will pour as much of our money as it can into Liberal ridings before the next election in order to stem the Tory tidal wave. If last year was the year of the dog according to my Chinese friends, this year will be the year of the pork barrel. Let me give the House a few examples.
The centrepiece of the Special Recovery Program announced in the budget is the $2.2. billion capital projects fund. Control of this pork barrel will be in the hands of a special Cabinet committee. The same people who brought us Canadair, Consolidated Computer, Coalgate and the National Energy Program now have a lot more mad money.
Even though they are the cornerstone of the Government's job creation effort, the projects announced so far have contained few job estimates. Numbers that have been provided have proved to be inflated and grossly misleading. For example, the Government announced that it will be spending $147 million to purchase 20 Canadair CL-215 water bombers in order to develop a national firefighting fleet. In the original announcement, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) said that 650 jobs per year would be created through this measure. In fact, the Government is committed to purchasing only four of these water bombers and has bought two of them for the Yukon where the fire season starts before the ice is out of the

lake. That is another example of forward planning and fast tracking. The other 16 will be bought only if the Provinces agree to buy a matching 16 planes. Since the Provinces have never been eager to foot the extremely high cost of this plane, the purchase of all 36 planes is far from assured. Some Provinces have indicated that they are not interested since their terrain is not suited to this particular aircraft.
Even if orders are placed for the full complement of planes, Canadair has told us that the Government's job estimates are grossly inflated. In fact, no jobs would be generated this year at all. Canadair is actually laying off people this summer. By January, 1984, if all the planes go ahead, 155 jobs may be created. By May, 1984, assuming all of the planes go ahead, 300 jobs may be created. By December, 1984 that number will rise to 525 jobs, and it will not be until the peak of production in June, 1985 that there will be the 650 jobs associated with this project as suggested by the Minister.
Similarly, the Government announced it would be spending an additional $185 million on the coastguard and generate 20,000 jobs in the process. This job figure has turned out to be grossly exaggerated. A much more realistic estimate is that approximately 2,000 jobs may result some time in the future.
While little effort has been made to provide accurate job forecasts for these projects, elaborate attention has been paid to staging the announcement to garner maximum attention. Despite the program's claim that it will provide immediate economic and employment opportunities throughout Canada, it is clear that its major goal is maximum political development for the Liberal Party rather than maximum economic development for Canadians.
Similarly, the Minister responsible for regional and economic expansion announced a restructuring of the programs in his Department last week. The intention of the new Industrial and Regional Development Program he said, is to distribute federal financing assistance more effectively than before. I would be most interested in the Minister's definition of "effective", but I can guess that he means he has devised a better way to channel money into Liberal ridings. The Minister calls it targeting.
In deciding what region will receive federal money, the country is divided into its 260 census districts. A formula called a development index will be applied in order to determine the level of assistance. The index will be based on three factors: the rate of unemployment in the census district; the level of income per person in the district; and the fiscal capacity of the Province in which the district is located. That means the ability of that Province to raise money.
At first glance it all looks very objective. It does not take much analysis, however, to uncover some real difficulties with this approach. For example, the same size for determining the unemployment rate in each district, if it is based on the labour force statistics, will be too small to be reliable. Even if this measurement were accurate, it would not take account of overall employment. In other words, it would not consider how many people have dropped out of the labour force. The data will therefore be skewed away from areas with high seasonal
unemployment which are just the areas that can benefit the most from programs such as these.
A more accurate measure of unemployment might take account of the number of people registered at Manpower or collecting Unemployment Insurance Benefits. Furthermore, the index will draw on data dating back to 1976 in order to focus on areas with historical levels of high unemployment and low income. Unfortunately, this does not permit a quick response to changing circumstances. It will work against my own Province of British Columbia, for example, which has been very hard hit by the recent recession. By factoring in the fiscal capacity of Provinces, the program will discriminate against hard-hit areas of relatively well off Provinces, such as Alberta, British Columbia and Ontario. Theoretically, every riding would qualify for some federal money. In this way the Government may find it a lot easier to inject money into favoured ridings which would not have qualified under the earlier programs designed to alleviate regional disparity.
The Minister has not said precisely how the formula will work, but the Government's past track record, for example with ILAP and the Canadian Community Development Program, suggests it will be jigged to work in favour of Liberal ridings. We in the Opposition want to know if the formula will be legislated or whether it will be left to ministerial discretion. We can only hope that it will operate at least a little more objectively than the Special Employment Incentives Program which has just received an infusion of $150 million over two years in the recent budget. This money is to be spent on the following:
Localized, employment intensive projects under existing Government construction and other programs.
So far we have had Liberal Senators, such as Senator Olson and Senator Argue, announcing funding for swimming pools and community arenas. But there is no formal application process for this money, so we cannot tell on what basis these successful projects were selected. It certainly is a "special" employment initiatives program. We do not know what criteria these projects must meet to qualify. We do not know how many jobs they will generate. We do not know how many go to which Provinces, and we do not know what the cost per person-year of employment is for each job created. But we know who announces them-Liberal Senators.
What is important are the economic consequences of the Government's actions. We have just been through the worst recession in 50 years, a recession that has inflicted hardship on millions of Canadians. The Government says that its policies are designed to ensure recovery takes place and that it lasts. Sadly, its policies are liable to have the opposite effect.
The result of this Government's actions may be to choke off recovery just as it gets started. As we pointed out in our official response to the budget, the Government is making no attempt to restrain spending even though its expenditures jumped by 17 per cent last year. It is true that the Government promises to keep its spending in line with increases in GNP,
May 5, 1983

but this means that the Government's share of the economy, which increased during the recession, will not decrease with recovery.
The Minister of Finance claims that there was nothing of substance in the official response to the budget. I would like to review exactly what I said because my comments are now being echoed by many other analysts. I pointed out that the Minister is making no attempt to restrain spending. Indeed, he plans to increase expenditures to help pay for his recovery program. I outlined the impact on social programs which are threatened by the runaway spending. Unless we can balance the books, there will be no money to pay for the social programs upon which Canadians depend. I also pointed out the divergence between the Government's fiscal and monetary policies. Sustained recovery will depend upon lower interest rates, but the increasing deficit threatens to crowd out the private sector incentives the budget is supposed to encourage as recovery takes hold. We cannot prevent interest rates from rising again in light of the Minister's deficit projection; the result will be a choking off of the recovery just as it gathers steam.
I also reviewed the budget's effects on various sectors of the economy. For example, I pointed out that it is not as favourable to business as it may at first appear. Certainly small business does not stand to gain very much, and that is a pity since approximately 32 per cent of new jobs in the country are created by that sector. Unfortunately, many small businesses were so weakened by the recession that they will not be able to take advantage of the investment incentives announced in the budget. Those incentives are not particularly useful to small businesses anyway; large businesses are more apt to use them. Of more use to small businesses would have been the adoption of the small business corporation which would have allowed them to increase their equity and improve their cash flow. This would have relieved the cash flow problems by allowing small businesses to take in partners who could write off losses against their income.
All businesses will be hurt by the tremendous tax increases which will be levied on consumers over the next four years. In fact, taxes will be increased by $5.7 billion by 1986. Increased spending by consumers is the principal need of small business. Unfortunately, consumption is liable to be reduced by the budget measures.
I reviewed many of the tax increases, including the elimination of the $100 standard deduction, the restructuring of the federal tax credit, the freezing of the children's exemption, the maintenance of the Canadian ownership charge, and the increase in the manufacturers' sales tax. The impact of many of these taxes will be regressive. Low and middle income Canadians will be the hardest hit.
We made all these points on the day after the budget was presented in the House. Now others are beginning to realize what the real impact of the budget will be. Thomas Maxwell, the Chief Economist of the Conference Board, has warned that the recovery is likely to stall by the end of next year. In a recent interview he said:
Borrowing Authority
Essentially what we see is enough momentum generated to keep us growing into 1984. The question is what happens towards the end of 1984 and into 1985. That I think is where our forecast and Lalonde's forecast start to part company. Because in our forecast, the economy sort of comes to a screeching halt in 1985 and 1986 as the very high interest rates combined with the tax increases associated with the later years of the budget start to put a constraint on growth.
Roger Keane of Midland Doherty said:
It is a mistake to view this as a pro-business budget; what it really has is all the attributes of a budget in which new public expenditures are brought down off the shelf.
I noticed today that Thomas D'Aquino who speaks for a group of businessmen is echoing our concern that business is being set up as the fall-guy in the budget, if they are unable to respond to the tax incentives it will provide the Government with a chance to intervene in the economy again.
I understand why people welcome the budget of the Minister of Finance compared with the three previous Liberal budgets. But this borrowing Bill only underlines the points I have been making about the economic mismanagement we have endured and will continue to endure under the Liberal Government.
Let us put this Bill into context. Over the past 15 years Government spending has ballooned by nearly 700 per cent. Just since the Liberal re-election in 1980, spending has increased 84 per cent on a national accounts basis. Government spending is now equal to 26 per cent of Canada's Gross National Product.
The Government argues that it must keep up its level of spending in order to combat the problem of unemployment in the country. But if one looks at historic levels of Government spending and their impact upon unemployment, it is clear that simply throwing more money at the problem solves nothing. For example, in 1970-71 the deficit stood at about $370 million and the unemployment rate ran at 5.7 per cent. In 1975-76 the deficit was $5.4 billion and the unemployment rate was close to 7 per cent. Today, with a projected deficit of over $31 billion, the unemployment rate tops 12 per cent. If we look at the projections of $25 billion per year budget deficits and unemployment rates of well over 10 per cent, we can see that running deficits does not help create employment and that there seems to be a distinct linkage between the size of the deficit and the increase in the unemployment rate. It is clear that this approach has not worked in the past and will not work in the future.
What do we need? We need to hold the Government accountable. The Government must explain its need for these additional funds. For it to be accountable, it must regain control of its expenditures. The Government cannot be permitted to inflate its borrowing authority in order to avoid returning to Parliament to explain how the money will be spent. We must oppose this Bill because it allows the Government to borrow far more money than it needs. The country cannot afford fiscal cushions for incompetent economic managers or election slush funds for desperate Liberals. We must keep in mind who will be paying the bill for this legislation.
At I said at the outset, it will be our children and grandchildren who will be saddled with the burden of excessive taxation

May 5, 1983
Borrowing Authority
unless we do something now. Unless we rein in Government expenditures, we will never as a nation achieve the level of prosperity we once enjoyed, nor will we have the capacity to adapt to the economic challenges of the 1980s. As I said, we may not even be able to afford the social programs to protect those who need it most. We will not be able to exploit our natural advantages in order to compete successfully in world markets. Our children will never enjoy the standard of living we have had. It is a grim outlook for the future-that is the real Liberal legacy.
It need not be this way. As our Party has stated, Canadians have the best chance right now to capitalize on our advantages, to be productive and competitive. The effects of the recession have been wrenching. However, those who survived are leaner, more efficient, more realistic. Excess capacity has been wrung out of the system. Faced with shrinking domestic markets, we have begun to look outward to promote our products in world markets to a greater extent. Many firms have reduced their oppressive debt loads and are ready to produce and be innovative again. Workers who have lost their jobs are beginning to think of retraining for new positions or starting their own businesses.
If we are to guarantee a recovery, we must be alert to new possibilities, aware of past mistakes and eager to adjust to changing circumstances. We must identify areas for improvement. For example, a survey conducted by the European Management Forum ranks 22 countries according to a range of factors, such as their productivity, industrial efficiency and human resources. It outlines Canada's advantages. We rank third in human resources, second with our natural resources and infrastructure, seventh in economic dynamism and sixth in competitiveness.
The survey also identifies an array of weaknesses. We are thirteenth in industrial efficiency; seventeenth in outward orientation or the will and ability to promote trade; sixteenth out of 22 in innovative forward orientation, which is the commitment to research and development and human resource development. We are in last place in employee productivity trends; and last again in export flexibility. Over-all we rank sixth. We should rank higher.
We must start working on these problems. We must improve our productivity and our competitiveness. We can no longer rely on our natural resource exports to ensure our prosperity and position in the world. We can no longer indulge in regional factionalism. We must use our regional diversity as a strength. We must develop an economic strategy that emphasizes the assets of each region, such as Canada's place on the Pacific Rim, and co-ordinate the actions of each level of Government to achieve this aim. We must address the problems of various economic sectors in the economy, such as energy and fisheries which have been ignored or abused by this Government. We must work to improve our management-labour relations.
These are just a few of the positive steps we should be taking. To ensure recovery, we must increase our markets. To increase our markets, we must increase consumer demand. We
can achieve increased demand by putting people back to work. To put people back to work, we must increase our export markets. To do that, we must be more competitive. To become more competitive, we must become more productive. To become more productive, we must expand our technological research and more aggressively apply it to industrial production.
To take these actions, we must change our attitudes and patterns of behaviour. It is an exciting challenge for us. A Government that demonstrates it is tackling these problems with determination, tenacity, co-operation and leadership will inspire confidence. That is what Canadians are looking for. That is what Conservatives can provide. That is why we will be proposing two amendments to this Bill at the appropriate time.
We believe the Government must account for all the money that is borrowed in its name. That is why we will be seeking to amend this Bill to include the financial requirements of Crown corporations. We believe the Government should seek authority to borrow only as much money as it needs. That is why we will be proposing an amendment to reduce the borrowing authority granted to half the amount that is currently being requested. We want to hold this Government to account. It must begin to control its expenditures. This Bill is a good place to start.

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1983-84 (NO. 2) MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Bill before us today asks for an additional $14.7 billion in borrowing authority. The Minister kindly explained to the House that $4 billion will be for a contingency fund. As the House knows, this is in addition to the contingency fund and borrowing authority granted to the Government in February when Bill C-143 was introduced and eventually passed through this House. That Bill authorized the Government to borrow an additional $19 billion. A short two months later, we are being asked to grant authority to borrow an additional $14.7 billion.
There will be a great many questions the Government will have to answer. As I said, the Minister did explain the proposed use of $4 billion in contingency funds. He said in part it was to meet runs on the Canadian dollar. He referred to the occasion in the last couple of years when the Government found itself spending $9.1 billion in an effort to stabilize the Canadian dollar. He also pointed out the Government wanted to avoid having to trigger unusual methods of financing by using Section 39 because of the effects this sort of action has on the stock market and money markets, not only in this country but around the world.
Having just received a budget statement from this Government, we must now ask what the money will be used for. We can speculate. There will be some increases in costs. Unemployment is at a record high, and therefore funds being drawn out of the Unemployment Insurance Fund will continue to increase. Part of this borrowing authority will probably be used to cover the resulting deficit.
As people have more difficulty finding a job and as their Unemployment Insurance benefits run out, more and more of
May 5, 1983

them are forced on to welfare in order that they and their families can subsist. The federal Government pays about half the welfare cost. Given the present economic conditions, some of this money will be used to offset these calls on the federal Treasury. As well, there will be continuing interest costs to cover the very high Government expenditures. While interest rates have dropped for the Government as well as for the rest of us, the volume of money being borrowed by Government continues to rise.
We note from the budget material that the usual revenues that offset the high cost of these federal programs will not be received to the same extent. Revenues from energy taxation will be down because of the reduced demand due to current economic conditions. The energy demand has dropped between 15 per cent and 18 per cent. Therefore, revenues from that source are down even though the Government attempted to maintain the oil compensation charge which it promised to drop at the beginning of this year.
Another area where normal Government revenues are expected to carry the show, so to speak, is in the area of personal income tax. As more and more people become unemployed, there will be less goods and services and less people paying income tax. The take from that source will be down as well. The take in corporate income taxes will likely drop because of economic conditions and because the budget further reduces the level at which corporations are taxed. In fact, I think one of the main thrusts of the budget is to create an impact upon the Government, causing it to come before us for additional borrowing authority.
There is now a continuation of the policy that both Liberal and Conservative Governments have embarked upon over the last 25 or 30 years. It is a continuation of the policy of increasing taxation for individuals and reducing taxation for corporate citizens. In the late 1950s, the revenue from income tax was approximately 50-50, half coming from corporations and half coming from private individuals. I should point out that in the early 1950s, close to 70 per cent of the revenue was from corporations and only 30 per cent was from individuals. By the end of the 1950s it had gone to a 50-50 basis. At the end of the 1970s approximately 30 per cent of income tax was paid by corporations and about 70 per cent by individuals.
Since we are talking about the difficulty the Government has keeping a large enough cash flow and since we are talking about raising funds, I would be remiss if I did not point out that there are a lot of deferred corporate taxes that have accumulated in this country. That deferred corporate tax is almost enough to cover the deficit that the Government has accumulated for the people of Canada.

speechtext:
I believe it would cover about half of it; between $60 billion and $70 billion in deferred taxes versus the $130 billion to $140 billion accumulated deficit of the federal Government.
Using my own personal favourite corporate taxpayer, Canadian Pacific Limited, as an example of what this means,
Borrowing Authority
Canadian Pacific has deferred taxes in the neighbourhood of $1.6 billion. There are no Canadian studies which will indicate, and we do not know from Canadian experience, how much of these deferred taxes will ever find their way into the revenues of the Government. We do know that studies in the United States indicate that less than 5 per cent of deferred corporate taxes are ever collected and find their way into the revenues of the federal Government. For practical purposes, we can say that those deferred taxes are tax gifts to that particular sector of the economy. Discontinuing that sort of practice would leave the federal coffers in much better shape because there would be approximately half as much money paid out in interest to maintain the level of debt that must now be maintained.
I would like to make a few remarks concerning the way the budget has addressed the problems of the advantaged and the disadvantaged in our society. It is relevant to discuss this now at a time when there are something in the neighbourhood of 1.6 million to two million individuals in Canada who are unemployed and looking for jobs. These people have no work but they still have the daily costs incurred to maintain themselves with warmth and shelter and food and clothing. They are still trying to educate their children and provide some means of enabling the next generation to survive in Canadian society.
It is my belief that the budget failed miserably in addressing the rift that is growing between the advantaged and the disadvantaged in our society. I say this because it seems to me that the only tax breaks offered in the budget were tax breaks to upper income earners. As the budget is being analyzed more and more, I think the consensus now among most of the tax analysts is that individuals with incomes in the $60,000 and up income bracket have received a fairly substantial tax break from the budget.
The Globe and Mail, in an article on May 3, said it as succinctly as it could be said. The headline stated:
"Low, middle income earners losers: analysis of a regressive budget." I do not think the budget can be called anything other than regressive when uppper income earners who have the ability to pay a higher proportion of income tax are given a break while the lower and middle income earners are having some of the tax relief that was previously available to them gradually eroded.
As a case in point, I bring to the attention of the House the $200 tax relief that was introduced last year which is being reduced by $100 this year. Apparently, the budget papers tell us that that will be eroded by another $50 next year and will be phased out completely by about 1986. That tax break was previously offered to low and middle income earners in an attempt to increase total demand in the economy.
It is our Party's analysis that the only way this economy can get back in gear and back on the road is to introduce a tax policy that will allow middle and low income earners to increase their expenditures and their demand so that there will

May 5, 1983
Borrowing Authority
be a market created for goods and services, thereby putting more people back to work. This would create more investment as well and would make the preparations necessary to return to full employment in the society.
Another small provision in the budget that we see as being regressive is the changes to the child cost allowance. This must be put into perspective. The change purports to create an increase for families or individuals who are maintaining children, but the big question that has not been properly answered by anyone from the Government side that I am aware of is what happens to the availability of that money if one or both parents are suddenly left unemployed? The interpretation we seem to have at this time is that if one or both of the people raising children in a normal family are left without a job, there is then no reason to have child care costs as part of the family budget because one person will be at home. It has been forgotten that that unemployed person should not be at home but should be spending time looking for a new job. It appears to us from our interpretation of the budget that that child care allowance will no longer be made available to them.
Again, the budget is regressive. The people who need the tax break, the people who have lost their jobs and could benefit from an additional $1,000 tax break, will have that withdrawn. As well as being left unemployed, these people will take a further loss by losing a tax advantage that they thought they had at the beginning of the year.
To accentuate further the rift in the Government's attitude toward the advantaged and the disadvantaged, there is the Indexed Securities Investment Plan, the ISIP. We have here, according to the budget papers, an attempt by the Government to encourage investment. Indeed, it may encourage some kinds of investments. As I said earlier, the kind of income earner who is best able to take advantage of an ISIP will be someone with a fairly large income, probably in excess of $40,000 or $50,000 a year, because an ISIP must be set up somewhat like the old Registered Home Ownership Plan. A plan must be established through a trust company or an insurance company or some such agency. The assets that are put into such a plan can only be stock purchased on the regular open stock market. It seems to me that this is drawing a very curious line between small individual investors, people who run their own small businesses or farms, or people who may even be incorporated running a family corporation not offered on the stock market. This is setting up two levels of investors, consistent with Government policy, I guess. The Government seems to be hellbent on setting up two classes of people in this country, the very rich and the very poor.
As I read the program, the Government is setting up a two-tier attitude when it comes to taxing capital gains. Those people who set up an ISIP get some advantage. They get a good chunk of their capital gain written off. They can absorb the gain and transfer it into income at a later date, perhaps when they are ready to retire. But a small-businessman or a farmer is still tied to a V-day of 1971. A person setting up an ISIP gets a V-day of 1983. At the end of each year he can
review his portfolio and pay only 25 per cent of his capital gain. The rest is rolled over and he gets the advantage of it. There is an inflation index written into the ISIP which the small-businessman, the farmer or the holder of a small private corporation does not have the benefit of.
We see with this budget a total ignoring of the small people who are actually the fuel and main motor of the economy. The investor in common stocks, with all due respect to the Government, does not provide that much of an incentive. He or she is not providing a whole lot of expertise for the building and the growth of the economy. All they are doing is plunking some money on the line and hoping the people managing the affairs of that common stock company will, in fact, invest in something which will grow.
When I look at the investment choices of some of these large entities that are financed through common stock, it seems to me, from recent history at least, that the trend has not been to create new investment, to shoot off into new fields, with perhaps the possible exception of the computer and high-tech industry, but to amalgamate. For example, there was the Hudson's Bay Company and the Simpson's and Zellers operation of a few years ago. Very large operations, instead of using surplus funds to create new jobs and new enterprises, amalgamate existing enterprises and do away with some of the competition they had. At the same time they do away with an awful lot of jobs.
I think the new investment policy which the Government outlined in the budget does not make it at all clear where the investment should take place. The Government talked about 100 different programs around the country on budget night. We still hear Government Members using the number of programs but we are not seeing any announcements of where the investments will be and where these great projects are going to take place. It is a particularly good question to be asking, Mr. Speaker, because we note with interest that plant capacity in this country is running around 60 per cent or slightly lower.
Faced with that reality, what reason is there for an investor to rush out, build a new plant or wreck an old plant and build a new one? There may be some industries where that might happen. When it does happen, as it does occasionally in the high-tech industry, the plant created as a result requires fewer not more people, and it does not lead to an increase in employment. Touting this particular budget as a budget that will bring about recovery and employment through increased employment and creating demand is a dream and an illusion which the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) would have us believe. He has not presented any facts. There is no factual material accompanying those allegations to show us that what he says will happen will happen.
I would now like to speak about the use the federal Government is making of its moneys. It is pertinent because the Government is asking us for another $16.7 billion in borrowing authority. The last few moments of my time I will talk about the Government's program for railway redevelopment in this
May 5, 1983

country. What the Government is proposing to do is throw $3 billion-something at the railways to do some double-tracking and to complete a tunnel needed in the mountains on the eastern slopes of the Rockies. The Government is alleging that this will solve a problem which it perceives concerning the movement of grain.
I will not spend a lot of time reminding the House that far less than 20 per cent of the total traffic on those rails is actually grain and that projections by the end of the 1990s would have that traffic as low as 10 per cent or 12 per cent. I simply want to talk about the manner in which the Government is proposing to spend the money. The Government is proposing to give that more than $3 billion to the railways with absolutely no strings attached. The Government is not proposing to take equity in the railways so the people of Canada can benefit if the railways are profitable and so Canadians can have some say in the decisions made at the board of directors level with respect to the Canadian Pacific side of the railway operation. The Government is not setting itself up for an eventual operation of that transportation system, which I think is legitimately a public utility kind of operation. It is the kind of operation that cries out, even under capitalistic economics and free enterprise thinking, to be an enterprise that is carried on for the public good and should be carried on for the benefit of the public.
The Government has instead decided to make the same mistakes that were made more than 100 years ago by providing funds to friends in the railway companies without taking back any equity. We think the funds would be better spent and better managed if the railways were required to increase their shareholding and capitalization, and Government funds go to pick up those increased shares. This would not result in an unexpected increase in the value of the shares currently held and it would have almost no effect on the profitability or nonprofitability of the earnings of the shareholders that now exist. It would allow the people of Canada to increase their control of what has traditionally been a privately controlled transportation conglomerate in this country.
By becoming more involved, we could eventually move to a situation where co-operation would exist between the two railways and avoid a great expenditure down the road for some of the double-tracking which is foreseen. This can be accomplished simply by co-operating rather than continuing the charade of competition. The Fraser Canyon, which is a very narrow access to Vancouver and the Lower Mainland of British Columbia, now has one railway operating on either side. If the two railways could ever be enticed into co-operating, one of those rails could be an outgoing line and the other could be an incoming line and capacity could be increased phenomenally-simply by co-operation. We are suggesting that if capital could go into the railways to increase their capacity, their equity capital, with control maintained on behalf of the people of Canada, and if eventually the Board could be controlled in the interests of the people of Canada, then that sort of co-operation would be greatly enhanced.

We see the economic proposals, the budgeting and the fiscal propositions which have been proposed to us by Government in the last week and here today as being very lacking in forward planning. They do not seem to have a plan for getting us out of this recession. There does not seem to be a clear decision made to try to reduce unemployment and increase demand for low and middle income workers so that the economy can get itself out of this recession. We find that the further call on this House to increase the borrowing authority by another $14.7 billion, virtually on the heels of a borrowing authority of $19 billion, further accentuates what we see as the ineptitude of this Government.

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1983-84 (NO. 2) MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is the seventh time in this session of Parliament that I have risen on behalf of our Party to speak to a borrowing authority Bill. The first Bill, you will recall, sir, was Bill C-30, a Bill to authorize the Government to borrow $12 billion. That was immediately followed up the following year by Bill C-59, a Bill requesting another $14 billion. Then, starting the fiscal year 1982-83, there was Bill C- 111 for $6.6 billion; then Bill C-125, originally for $11 billion and then down to $7 billion. There was then Bill C-128 for $4 billion; Bill C-143 for $19 billion. Now we have Bill C-151 for $14.7 billion. It seems to me that we are spending a great deal of the time of this session of Parliament debating borrowing authority Bills to feed the insatiable appetite of this Government for money or debt.
May I remind you, sir, that on March 31, 1980, roughly when this session of Parliament was about to commence following the 1980 election, the total net debt of the people of Canada was $72.1 billion. That included not only our debt denominated in Canadian dollars, but our debt denominated in foreign currency borrowings. The total amount was $72.1 billion. As of the end of this fiscal year which has just passed, March 31, 1983, the net debt has been moved to $115.8 billion. If this Bill and the borrowing requirements which are contemplated in the budget go through, the net debt of the country will be $142.5 billion by March 31, 1984. I can say to you, sir, that we have doubled the national debt of Canada in the very short period of time since the last election.
There is no justification for that kind of spending, that kind of mismanagement. There is no justification whatsoever. It would be totally improper for any Member of Parliament who loved his country, who had some concern for his kids, who had some concern for his neighbour's children, and their children's children, not to insist that there be some accounting for a program of debt which seems to have no end. This debt will have to be paid. It will have to be paid by my children, by my children's children, and indeed by their children's children. It goes on and on and on! We cannot excuse ourselves by saying: "Well, we are just going into a little bit of debt this year because we have a lot of people out of work and we must do some things to stimulate the economy", because that has not been the case. For part of the session of this Parliament, times are said to have been relatively good, certainly very much more relatively good than they are today. Yet Bills were presented

May 5, 1983
Borrowing Authority
for $12 billion and for $14 billion, and so on and so on. Therefore it is not a question of just bad times. It is not a question of just tough times now and let's borrow a little and stimulate the economy and get things going again. It is a situation where we have been borrowing both in good times and in bad times.
In that sense I want to go now to the budget itself and take a look at the projections of this Government. If one wants to talk about building confidence in Canada, borrowing authority Bills of this nature do everything but build confidence, although the budget contemplates an increase in the Gross National Product this year of 2.3 per cent in real terms; next year over 5 per cent in real terms; the following year 4.4 per cent and continuing to 4.7 per cent in real terms. In other words, according to the budget Canada is about to enter into great boom times.
But then you must look at the borrowing and the deficit requirements. You find that forever, as far as you can see down the road, we are going to have deficits in excess of $25 billion and borrowings of between $25 billion and $30 billion. How can we possibly have confidence when in times which are supposed to be boom times, times when there is real growth in the economy, where the economy is growing faster, as projected by the budget, than at any time since the War, we have a situation where we will forever have deficits? The fact of the matter is that the budget and its projections are total garbage. They mean nothing. They will lead us to disaster, because as Government borrows it sucks up money from the system and prevents that money from being used by those who create wealth-because Government creates no wealth-and as it does that it drives interest rates up.
I point out to you, sir, that while interest rates may seem, in comparison to 1981 and 1982, to be down now, and likely to be down again when the Treasury bill auction takes place later today, real interest rates-and I am talking about the difference between what is the true inflation and what interest we are paying-are probably higher today than they have been at any time in the past three years.
If we look at the projected inflation rate, not the current inflation rate, and if we look at the projected increase in wholesale prices, we find that the real interest rate, the rate between what is deemed to be the inflation rate and the rate which the banking system charges at prime, today at 11 per cent, is between 8 per cent and 9 per cent. That is an enormous burden. We are only paying that rate of interest because Governments, particularly this one, are borrowing far more than they can legitimately take out of the economy. If the economy improves, as the Government suggests in this budget it will, then I can tell you, sir, that the improvement will not in fact take place because interest rates will go to the moon.
When we look at this Borrowing Authority Bill, we must look at what it does to business confidence and what it says about the financial affairs of the country and the creation of the enthusiasm and drive necessary to make the country work
better. The Government in its budget says it needs $26.7 billion to finance its requirements for the year. The Government says that as of the first of the fiscal year, April 1, it had borrowing capacity of $16 billion, so it would seem to need an additional capacity to borrow of only $10.7 billion. However, the Minister says: "I need a contingency. I am not satisfied with the gross amount of $26.7 billion; that does not give me any contingency." That is bare bones, he says.
Well, sir, that cannot be. The Minister talks about foreign exchange problems but he knows when he borrows in foreign markets that money is converted into Canadian dollars, so it does not matter whether he borrows abroad or in Canada. The fact is that the budget says he can get along on $26.7 billion, including contingencies. He says: "I need another $4 billion on top". That is less than three weeks after he produced the budget. And the people of Canada are supposed to have confidence in this Government's financial management, after it says on April 19 it needs $26.7 billion and on May 5 it says it needs $30.7 billion!

On anything over that amount on deposit the Government gets interest from the chartered banks at a rate roughly 10 per cent less than the going Treasury bill rate. subtopic: CROWSNEST PASS RATE-OPPOSITION TO PLAN FOR CHANGE
CROWSNEST PASS RATE-OPPOSITION TO PLAN FOR CHANGE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, in 1897 the Crow rate, with an average cost of one-half cent per ton mile, to move grain by railway from the Prairies was established. Under the Crow rate, grain production prospered, billions of dollars in foreign exchange were earned, and the railways made money. Cow-calf producers, feed lot operators, meatpacking plants and secondary grain processors continued to flourish because the distortion did not affect the over-all natural advantage of western agriculture.
During the late 1960s and the 1970s, due to inflation brought on by the present Liberal Cabinet, the Crow rate became a major distortion between grain producers on one hand and the livestock industry and the secondary grain processing industry on the other. The over-all natural economic advantage was lost. In 1982 the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) created the Gilson consultative process to negotiate a reasonable solution. Nine major farm organizations, the two national railways, and one group of processing companies spent thousands of hours negotiating an over-all compromise.
The Minister of Transport has since made major changes to the compromise whereby the major economic distortions are still in existence. The over-all balance and fairness have been lost. All of this happened without Members of the House ever seeing any legislation or being able to contribute our knowledge and experience.
Surely this whole process shows once again how incredibly incompetent the present Liberal Government is, whereby the nation must once again endure the worst of all possible solutions.

subtopic: AMOUNTS PAID IN QUEBEC COMPARED WITH OTHER PROVINCES
AMOUNTS PAID IN QUEBEC COMPARED WITH OTHER PROVINCES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it is often said in the media, in this House and also in the National Assembly that Quebecers pay the highest taxes in Canada. I thought Canadians and Quebecers would be interested in some information on income tax levels in the various provinces. For instance, a taxpayer with a taxable income of $6,000 will pay $1,496 in income tax in Quebec, $1,119 in Ontario-$377 less-and $906 in Alberta-$590 less. With a taxable income of $25,000, our taxpayer will pay pay $9,229 in Quebec, but would pay $2,098 less in Ontario and $2,569 less in Alberta. I think that these figures speak for themselves, and that all the rhetoric of politicians who are "all talk and no action" is losing much of its impact on the people of Quebec.
Those are real reasons why investors are avoiding Quebec. These are factors over which the Government of Quebec has complete control, and therefore it cannot blame its neighbours or the Government in Ottawa. In fact, Mr. Parizeau will have a chance to remedy the situation next Tuesday when he brings down his budget.

speechtext:
Madam
Speaker, the Solicitor General (Mr. Kaplan) proposes to release earlier, for the first-time, offenders convicted for nonviolent offences. We all agree that the need is to get some prisoners out of jail, but only if they are genuinely rehabilitated and not likely to be a danger to the public. We need more qualitative release, not quantitative release. How do we accomplish that? We are obviously not accomplishing it presently.
Rehabilitation is essentially the responsibility of the individual, I believe. We cannot wave a magic wand and have automatic rehabilitation. Only an individual man or woman can rehabilitate himself or herself through their own voluntary change of mind and heart.
The Solicitor General and the Parole Board Chairman are reported as saying that there will be no change in the basic screening process for release. Surely, this is the real point, to determine where we can make a bold move to achieve both genuine rehabilitation and a reduction in the number of prisoners.
Why can we not change the existing process of screening to a meaningful process of qualifying, and put the onus and responsibility for qualifying on the individual prisoner?

May 5, 1983
We should not have to screen him or her. If prisoners want to get out, they should take the initiative and pass the test of satisfying the Parole Board that they have changed their lives enough to qualify for release. If there is a doubt about this, it should be resolved in favour of the community.
We shall only reduce crime effectively when we tackle the causes, not the symptoms of crime.

subtopic: THREAT TO EMPLOYMENT-MINISTER'S STATEMENT
THREAT TO EMPLOYMENT-MINISTER'S STATEMENT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the Minister of Economic Development (Mr. Johnston) has me worried because he has told us all not to worry. The Minister calmly assures us that an additional two million workers thrown out of work by technology, in addition to the two million now without work or hope, will not be a tragedy. That has me worried.
The Minister says, "Do not worry, put your faith in the private enterprise system, the system will provide." That has me more worried.
When the mechanization of agriculture drove workers off the land, they adjusted by finding work in factories. When the automation of industry drove workers from the factories, they adjusted by finding work in offices and the service sector. Now, computers and micro electronics will drive workers off to nowhere. There is no place left to go.
It is true that we cannot and should not hold back the tidal wave of technology that is about to engulf us. We must join in on the micro electronic revolution, or be swept away. But we must join in on our own terms and in ways that will benefit ordinary people. The Minister's "technology at any costs" vision is blurred by panic.
There are other visions. Some of us, like the Catholic Bishops, see alternatives that would place the emphasis on socially useful forms of production, labour intensive industries, the use of appropriate forms of technologies.
Given such alternatives we would not only survive, we would even prosper as the new wave of technology washes over us. The Minister may think that he has all the answers. The worry is: has he even understood the question?

subtopic: SUGGESTED APPOINTMENT OF ROYAL COMMISSION
SUGGESTED APPOINTMENT OF ROYAL COMMISSION
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, under the new Canadian Constitution, new Provinces can only be formed and provincial boundaries can only be extended with the approval of seven Provinces having 50 per cent of the Canadian population. Any Province can accept or veto any changes to its boundaries, under Section 43.
There exists no criteria for creating new Provinces or for changing the boundaries of any Province. Therefore, Parliament should appoint a Royal Commission at the earliest opportunity to recommend criteria for such changes. Indeed, criteria should be established for the granting of provincial status to the Yukon, the granting of semi-provincial status to the Mackenzie region, the possible establishment of new Provinces within the central region of Canada, and the possible extension of provincial boundaries north of the sixtieth parallel into the northern Territories. The creation of additional Provinces would enhance national unity and provide greater equity to the entrenched constitutional amending formula.
May 5, 1983

speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of State for Economic Development. Yesterday I challenged him to an open debate with regard to technological change and job loss.
