subtopic: QUESTIONS ON THE ORDER PAPER
subsubtopic: CANADA-CZECHOSLOVAKIA DUAL NATIONALS
speechtext:
1.	Since 1977, how many employees of (a) the Government (b) Crown corporations and agencies (i) applied to the authorities of the Czechoslovak Socialist Republic for "regularization" of their legal relationship to that state in accordance with the decree of the Government of the Czechoslovak Socialist Republic of March 16, 1977 (ii) were consequently released from Czechoslovak citizenship (iii) were issued Czechoslovak passports (iv) travelled to the C.S.S.R. on Czechoslovak passports?
2.	What were the names of such employees and what positions did they occupy in the Public Service?
3.	Is it the policy of the Government to employ former citizens of Czechoslovakia who, according to the decree of the Government of the C.S.S.R. of March 16, 1977, while in Canada, renewed their allegiance to that State by signing a statement binding them "to behave and conduct themselves as citizens of the Czechoslovak Socialist Republic" or who were released from Czechoslovak citizenship by virtue of not having acted "in a way hostile to the Czechoslovak Socialist Republic or in a way damaging the interests of the Czechoslovak Socialist Republic"?
4.	Is it the policy of the Government to extend Canadian citizenship and/or Canadian residence to persons who claim to be refugees from the Czechoslovak Socialist Republic and who, subsequent to their landing in Canada, renewed their allegiance to the Czechoslovak Socialist Republic?

speakeroldname: Mr. David Smith (Parliamentary Secretary to President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
subtopic: QUESTIONS ON THE ORDER PAPER
subsubtopic: CANADA-CZECHOSLOVAKIA DUAL NATIONALS
speechtext:
I am informed by the Department of External Affairs, the Employment and Immigration Commis-sion/Department and the Public Service Commission as follows:
1.	This information is not available. Under the terms of Article 36 of the Vienna Convention on Consular Relations, to which both Canada and Czechoslovakia are party, Czechoslovak consular officials are free to communicate with and have consular access to individuals who are still deemed to be citizens of Czechoslovakia on matters which fall directly under their consular jurisdiction. This implies that in so doing, Czechoslovak consular officials are under no obligation to notify the Canadian Government of their legitimate contacts with Canadian-Czechoslovak dual nationals. At the same time, Canadian-Czechoslovak dual nationals are not obliged to notify the Canadian Government of their contacts with Czechoslovak consular officials. Therefore, unless the information is volunteered, which it usually is not, it is not possible for the Canadian Govenrment to compile data on those Canadian-Czechoslovak dual nationals who wish to comply with the Czechoslovak regulation.
Furthermore, all Canadian citizens and residents are free to leave Canada at will, and no person is required to inform the Government of his destination on leaving the country. No data on the movements of departing persons are maintained. It is therefore not possible to know accurately how many persons of Czechoslovak or other origin visited Czechoslovakia in any given period. This is equally true for all Canadians, regardless of employer.

May 5, 1983
Order Paper Questions
2.	For the reasons noted in Part 1 above, this information is not available.
3.	The Public Service Commission which is charged with the administration of the Public Service Employment Act does not have a policy which deals with the employment of former citizens of Czechoslovakia nor those of any other country. Former citizens of other countries, once having obtained Canadian citizenship, are entitled to compete for Government jobs on an equal basis with other Canadians. Should they not have obtained Canadian citizenship but be resident in Canada as landed immigrants they would still be able to compete for employment in the federal Public Service. The success of gaining such employment would be dependent on the application of certain provisions of the Public Service Employment Act. Thus in open competitions the Public Service Commission may restrict the selection to Canadian citizens when it is aware that there is a sufficient number of qualified Canadian applicants. A further provision of the Public Service Employment Act requires the Commission, when establishing an eligible list in open competitions, to list veterans and Canadian citizens ahead of non-citizens. In view of these provisions it is more difficult for landed immigrants who are non-citizens than for citizens to obtain federal Public Service employment.
There is no requirement for dual nationals to notify the Commission of the fact before seeking employment in the Public Service of Canada.
4.	In so far as the Immigration Act is concerned: Citizens and/or residents of Czechoslovakia may be accepted as refugees if they fall within the definition of "Convention Refugees" or those of the "Self-Exiled Persons Class".
Canada does not remove residence privileges status from Czechoslovak immigrants who come to Canada as refugees and who, once in Canada, renew their allegiance to the Czechoslovak Socialist Republic. As a signatory state to the 1951 Convention and the 1967 Protocol relating to the Status of Refugees, Canada ascribes to the Regulations laid down by the UN High Commissioner for Refugees on the acquisition or reacquisition of national protection by an individual. These Regulations state inter alia that:
If the refugee does not act voluntarily, he will not cease to be a refugee. If he is instructed by an authority, eg. of his country of residence, to perform against his will an act that could be interpreted as re-availment of the protection of the country of his nationality, such as applying to his consulate for a national passport, he will not cease to be a refugee simply because he obeys such an instruction. He may also be constrained, by circumstances beyond his control, to have recourse to a measure of protection from his country of nationality.
In so far as the Citizenship Act is concerned: Under the provisions of the Citizenship Act which became effective on February 15, 1977, naturalization as a citizen is a matter of qualified right subject to the requirements of the Act. Among these requirements are that the applicant making application therefor is: (1) 18 years of age or more, (b) has been admitted to Canada for permanent residence (as a landed immigrant by the Immigration authorities) and has since such admission, resided in Canada for at least three out of the four years immediately prior to date of application, (c) must not be under
order of deportation, and (d) must be free of the prohibitions to the grant of citizenship which pertain to criminal activity and security offences.
Persons of Czech nationality whether or not they have maintained and/or affirmed their allegiance to Czechoslovakia have been and will be granted Canadian citizenship in like manner to any other adult who makes application and satisfies all of the requirements to become a citizen.
In addition, under the terms of the 1977 Citizenship Act there are no statutory provisions for automatic loss of citizenship upon becoming a citizen of another country outside of Canada as had existed in the former Act (1947) and prior legislation. This change in law has increased the numbers and will continue to increase the numbers of dual national Canadians residing both inside and outside Canada. Those persons residing outside of Canada in their country of second nationality (example Czechoslovakia) or visiting there, especially those travelling on the passport of the second nationality, are considered to be subject to all of the laws of that country and may, for real or imagined infractions of the law, be prevented from leaving and in some cases may be imprisoned.

Borrowing Authority

Mr. Speaker, I intended and hoped to have the time to get into that very issue in my remarks. The Minister will realize that for over a year and a half we have suggested the appointment of a special committee of the House to have over-all supervisory budgetary control. That committee would inquire into and priorize Government expenditures in order to make sure that they would fit within the framework of how the Government and the House would deem these expenditures be spent. There are a number of expenditures that are made, all deemed to be necessary, but there is a need to priorize those expenditures.
We can only have in our household that which we can afford. While there are many things we would like, as Members of Parliament we eventually have to come to grips with what we can afford. We need the social nets that exist in health and welfare and we need to look after those least able to help themselves.
But, do we really need the PIP Program at this point? Do we really need the CHIP Program at this point? Do we really need to spend as much as we do on entertaining ourselves? Do we need the advocacy advertising at this point? Are there not many expenditures which may be desirable and great but not really needed at all at a time when we have economic dislocation and revenues cannot even come close to meeting budgetary demands? Do we not need to priorize our efforts and consider if it is really worth the interest cost to borrow the money to do that which may or may not be necessary?

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased with this opportunity to speak today to Bill C-151 and to the budget, which, I am convinced, will give Canadians the assurance that our economy is on the right track. I want to congratulate the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde), who before he brought down his budget, held a series of thorough and intensive consultations with the private sector, governments and various organizations. The budget will provide the necessary means for helping those who want to work but cannot find jobs. I am referring to young people and to older workers. What I really admire in this budget is that the Government wants to provide help for Canadians who need it most. This $4.8 billion recovery budget will, of course, help create jobs, especially in the private sector. I may add that more than $250 million in additional funds will be spent on expanding existing programs relating to housing, more specifically, the purchase, renovation and improvement of homes.
Mr. Speaker, in Verdun-Saint Paul, this program, in which the Canadian Government has invested a little over $2 million, has helped build about 100 co-operative housing units, the result being that many of my constituents now own their own homes and tenants living in units that have been renovated. That is why I am particularly pleased that the Minister agreed to increase the number of units to be built this year to 25,000, that is, new social housing units for low- and middle-income Canadians. This program was also instrumental in carrying out another very important building project in my riding, and I am of course referring to the senior citizens' home, on which more than $4 million has been spent by the Canadian Government, so that senior citizens will be able to move in by next July. As a result, 100 senior citizens on low incomes will be able to enjoy a comfortable and happy life.
While I am on the subject of housing, Mr. Speaker, I shall, if I may, express my appreciation to the Minister of Public Works (Mr. LeBlanc) for some programs that are very important to the people of Verdun-Saint Paul, and I am referring to
the Canadian Home Ownership Stimulation Plan and the Canadian Home Renovation Plan. About 100 of my constituents took advantage of these programs during 1982. From comments I have heard, I expect we shall be receiving many more requests in the coming year.
And what about the important changes in the Registered Home Ownership Savings Plan? In my view, this program will encourage many of my constituents to spend their savings on the purchase of a new home, furnishings and household appliances. It will also enable small contractors to start construction projects and, as a result, provide job opportunities for thousands of Canadians.
Mr. Speaker, as far as job creation is concerned, especially for young people, I am proud of the fact that the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy) has put at the disposal of Verdun-Saint Paul residents an information centre designed especially for young people. This centre will enable our youth to acquire vocational training and make it easier for them to make the transition to the labour market. Within three months, this centre has already enabled 150 graduates to find a regular job, which is very promising for the future of our young people. On the other hand, now that our economic woes are behind us as long as the Quebec Government does not make an effort to cooperate with its Canadian partners and as long as it insists on its independence priority, unfortunately very few businessmen will be willing to invest in Quebec.
The best proof of this was given by the Minister of Finance when he spoke before the Montreal Chamber of Commerce and was asked the following questions: Which Government is to blame for excessive taxes in Quebec? Who caused the headquarters of several companies to close down in Montreal? Which Government continues to promote uncertainty concerning the political future of Quebec? Members of this House will not learn anything new if I say that the Quebec Government alone is to blame. I believe that very few people remain blind to this fact and still say that the Quebec Government is not to blame. The only Government that does its best to create jobs and support industry in Quebec, to keep corporate headquarters in Montreal, to support major businesses and help to finance industrial modernization is the Canadian Government. If the Quebec Government persists in trying to separate the province from the rest of Canada, Quebecers will unfortunately be poorer in every respect, that is economically, socially and culturally. The only way for us to have a better future is for the Quebec Government to cooperate more seriously with the Federal Government.
I would like to call the attention of the House to the area of job creation. While the Canadian Government takes initiatives to create jobs, the provincial Government ignores young job seekers who, once again, are unable to benefit from federal assistance. For instance, last December, when the federal-provincial agreement was signed to implement the NEED
May 5, 1983

program and create thousands of jobs in various municipalities, the Quebec Government again reversed its decision and refused to sign the agreement at the last moment.
How can Canada prosper, Mr. Speaker, when the leaders of the Quebec Government are constantly trying to obstruct Federal initiatives and make the people of Quebec believe that Ottawa is responsible for our present economic problems?
Mr. Speaker, if this budget is to have any impact on the jobless, the private sector will have to take advantage of the programs implemented by the Canadian Government. I realize that the private sector has been under extreme pressures these last few years. That is why the Minister of Finance has provided special assistance for Canadian businesses. To this end, the budget contains measures which will allow businesses, especially small- and medium-size businesses, with much more limited resources, to get back in the saddle and reduce the indebtedness incurred by many of them. These businesses will then be able to use the money now required to finance their debt for more productive activities which will be more likely to create jobs. The $300 million provided to help businesses will allow them to bring their investments forward. Needless to say that, as investments increase in the private sector, as they must to guarantee a lasting long-term economic recovery, Government borrowings will decrease. Moreover, if the Government and the private sector use their resources to make our products more competitive, we shall be able to retain and increase our share of the market. Businesses must be encouraged to buy more of their supplies in Canada by promoting innovation and an increased productivity as well as new, larger and more modern production facilities. These are very important measures for putting the economy back on its rails, in a long-lasting effort to give Canadians permanent, meaningful and well-paid jobs.
It should be remembered, Mr. Speaker, that businesses in the Province of Quebec are at a serious disadvantage as against their competitors in other provinces, because of the shamefully high cost of energy in the Province of Quebec. Last week indeed, Mr. Parizeau's tax on gasoline accounted for 52 per cent of the price of a litre of gasoline in the greater Montreal area.
Mr. Speaker, 1 would also like to mention that I am interested in social issues as they relate to the constituency of Verdun-Saint-Paul, which has a rapidly ageing population. Without going into details, the Canadian Government has been successful in maintaining its social programs. I want to assure our senior citizens that, as far as I am concerned, I will go on making representations to the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) requesting further extensions to the existing social programs, in order that these people may still enjoy the same degree of protection.
Borrowing Authority
I also wish to congratulate the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) for his sensitivity to our people's expectations. This budget proposes changes in the child benefit system that will maintain the principle of universality, and programs aimed at low and middle-income families. Consequently, the budget will help single-parent families, mostly headed by mothers who usually make only 58 per cent of the salaries of men.
The child care expense deduction will be increased to $2,000 per child and to $8,000 per family, thus doubling the present deduction. This will certainly help low and middle-income families. Of course, the Child Tax Credit, which increased by $50 this year to help families, will be maintained and, in addition, when mothers claim their child tax credit, they will be entitled to a non-taxable amount of $343 for each child. I am also pleased that the $26,330 ceiling will remain unchanged and this child tax credit will still be paid in part to people whose income does not exceed $40,000. Again, I am fully satisfied that most families in need will be protected.

It is my sincere belief, Mr. Speaker, that all the measures introduced in the budget will serve the interests of all Canadians and give them confidence in the future.

To conclude, this is a budget to invest in, to work for and to build on. Through our efforts we can ensure that Canada moves not just from recession to recovery, but to lasting prosperity. The choice is ours.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to conclude on a humorous note. Since I first came here, I have been listening day after day to Opposition Members attacking the Government. Well, whatever they may say or do, people on this side are more efficient than the ones across the aisle.

A fierce debate is raging in the United States today over the magnitude of their deficit. This is a borrowing Bill and the Opposition is not suggesting by any means that the Government should not borrow money. Those of us in the Opposition realize, I believe, that the Government does have some legitimate reasons for needing to borrow money. It is certainly accepted that the Government should go to the market to borrow money. However, any concerned person, any concerned taxpayer of the country, must ask, when he is faced with the staggering amount of money which this Government is spending whether it is being spent properly. That is the concern, certainly, which I have, as well as all Members of the Opposition. One billion dollars represents $40 from each individual in the country. This year the Government is going to be running a deficit of $30 billion. That means that on behalf of each citizen in the country it will be borrowing $1,200. If you apply that to a family of four, it means that very close to $5,000 is being borrowed on behalf of that family. Therefore, if we in the Opposition are to be responsible in doing our job in representing those people who pay the taxes, and who are eventually going to have to bail out the Government, I believe we have to stand up and ask some legitimate questions as to how the Government is spending that money.
It goes back, Mr. Speaker, even further than budgets. In the Thirty-second Parliament, we are still in the first session. I fail to understand how any operation, whether it be a firm, a household, a farm or a business, can operate by running everything together. A farm, a business or a household operates on a period of time, a monthly basis, an annual basis or some such period of time. It seems to me that when this Government was elected in 1980, had it set out to have a Throne Speech each year, had it set out to have a budget each year, had it done some planning and presented Estimates on that basis, we would have had a much more sensible and sane way of spending and collecting money. What has happened though, is that in this one session of Parliament we have had seven separate borrowing Bills. In fact, it is almost like a rerun, a record which is stuck. This Government is continually asking the Parliament of Canada to approve more borrowings. As the Hon. Member for Calgary South pointed out, if some of this money is being used-which it is-for Government

There are other ways to run a deficit than collecting more money than you spend, which is exactly the kind of deficit this Government is riinning. There are other ways to run a deficit. One is to simply give incentives to private industry in the form of a forgoing of taxes over a period of time, whatever the Government thinks is appropriate. That would mean that you do not collect tax dollars, and in some ways that is a very real alternative to what the Government is doing. Rather than have tax dollars collected up front, and money borrowed up front and then given back to the private sector, maybe it should not collect the money in the first place but instead try to create some incentive. I feel that that would be a better way to run a deficit. That would increase the number of people working in this country and would in turn increase the amount of wealth which we create. That is another way we can look at in terms of how we can get ourselves out of the economic stagnation we are in, rather than simply having mass Government spending and mass Government borrowing and mass transfers of money from one sector to another. It does not take an economist, as the Hon. Member for Calgary South pointed out, to understand that. It is basic, simple common sense.
I heard an amusing description the other day, Mr. Speaker. I heard it said that Christopher Columbus was the first modern-day economist. It may be an old story but it is certainly ne^w to (^ne. When he started out to sail, he did not know where he was going. When he got to America, which turned out to be the new world, or was defined as the new world, he did not know where he was. When he got home, he did not know where he had been. And the reason he is a modern-day economist is that he did it all on Government money. That, in some ways, is the kind of fiscal policy which this Government has. There is no plan, it seems to me, other than to run up massive deficits.
If one looks at some of the accumulated deficits which we now have, I consider it almost scary. The national debt on a per capita basis in approaching $5,000. The amount of interest we are going to pay this year as an individual taxpayer to service that debt is $705. Relating that to an average family of four, it means that that family pays close to $3,000 in taxes which goes to service past Government debt. That does not finance any new schools. It does not allow for any additional transfer payments to Provinces. It does not fund any new programs. It simply goes to pay interest on past Government borrowings.

When mistakes are made and the Government is involved in the economy to that extent, it becomes a major problem. When you add that to what is going on in the provincial Governments, the average taxpayer in this country probably pays close to half of his total earnings to one level of Government or another in the form of taxes. It then becomes very, very important that those tax dollars are spent properly. If they are not, you simply create very large problems. It goes back to plain and simple common sense.

We have made suggestions and they may sound as if they were minor. When you are talking about a total budget of $80 billion, a million dollars does not sound like very much. But the point is that if you start looking for savings and come up with some useful suggestions and the Government could adopt them, then there is some incentive to save. Perhaps through saving $1 million here and $1 million there we can make a dent in the total spending. I come from an agricultural riding where it is very important that we be as competitive as we possibly can with other producers around the world. When you look south of the border, you find
that the American farmer is paying something like 40 cents or 50 cents a gallon less than the Canadian farmer. I have suggested repeatedly in the House, and I will say again because I see the Minister of State for Finance (Mr. Cosgrove) here and I hope he listens to me, that in Manitoba's case the federal Government collects a 7 cent a gallon tax on fuels used for the production of food on farms and then refunds it under certain conditions. The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fisher) is here and I hear him talking about wanting to fuel the private sector for recovery. Again, it is counterproductive.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to speak on the borrowing Bill because of some of the events which have been occurring in recent months and years and as late as yesterday, and which will be occurring over the next number of weeks and months. I want to relate borrowings by the Government for transportation purposes to the developments which have been taking place and which will continue.
I am not an economist nor a chartered accountant, however, it has always been my understanding that when Governments borrowed, they borrowed for specific purposes. I notice that the borrowing authority Bill does not tell us where the money is going in terms of specific and individual items. However, there is no doubt that much of those borrowings will go toward covering what could be called subsidies or direct grants. Much of it will also be devoted to capital investment purposes.
It has always been my understanding that Government revenues and expenditures incurred through borrowing used for such purposes as subsidies and grants to pay for things which bring no return and from which it is not possible to recover the moneys, are called dead weight debts. Those borrowings must be repaid out of future tax revenues of the Government. However, borrowings which are used for capital investment, whether it be airports, railways, seaways or seaports, can and should be called self-liquidating debts, in the sense that if money is provided for those purposes as repayable loans, they become self-liquidating debts. Or, if they are provided as a capital investment by the taxpayer, who originally borrowed the money through the Government, then surely the Government has a responsibility on behalf of the taxpayer to ensure that there is a return on the capital investment.
Does Your Honour know of anyone who would put up funds for capital investment without taking equity ownership, debentures, or bonds from which there was a return of interest and dividends? I do not know of any self-respecting investor or so-called free enterpriser who would hand out his own money or anyone else's without receiving some opportunity for return
on the investment, or at least being eligible for a return on the investment if it proved to be a successful one.
I am sure we could study many other areas of the economy, but we should consider the history in this country of borrowing funds for transportation purposes which were turned over to entrepreneurs for capital investments from which the people of Canada received little or no return. I suggest that it makes good, sound business sense that if one borrows money to invest in capital improvements, the money is used to get a return on that investment.
Since 1881, and probably before then for canals and small railways in central Canada, the people of Canada have provided capital investment for privately owned railroads as well as for land, forest, mineral rights and cash grants. They have provided funds for capital investment but did not own it.
We provided funds to take over bankrupt capital investments, such as in the formation of the Canadian National Railways. We took over five bankrupt railways, and while the banks and the bondholders got their money back, the taxpayers of Canada paid those debts and interest charges for the next 40 years approximately.
Incidentally, Canadian National was not formed because the Government of the day believed in a Crown corporation or publicly owned railway, but to bail out the bankrupt railways of Grand Trunk, Grand Trunk Northern, Grand Trunk Pacific, Canadian Northern and others. In the 1950s, 1960s and 1970s, those debts were transferred from Canadian National to the Government of Canada. In recent years there has been the odd year when Canadian National has paid a dividend to the single shareholder, the Government of Canada, because it was relieved of all these old debts and some recent ones and was able to show operating profits out of which it could pay a dividend and some income taxes. At least there was a beginning to some returns being made on that investment. I believe that is good beginning, but in recent years we have continued to hand money over for capital improvements or subsidies for which we have received no return.
In fact, some money was borrowed for these branch line subsidies. Not only did the railways expect the money for those branch line subsidies but they expected a return on those subsidies. In other words they expect a return for them on the taxpayers' money for the branch line subsidy.
The theory behind that subsidy, which included maintenance and depreciation, was that the railways would repair the branch lines. However, they did not do so, but kept the money. The Government introduced an additional program called branch line rehabilitation. A few hundred million dollars have gone into that program. The railways expect to get a 21 per cent return on that capital investment which the people of Canada gave them. That return is on the taxpayers' money, not the railroads'. They expect to get another 20 per cent for what is euphemistically called overhead.
May 5, 1983

A bureaucrat who appeared in front of the Transport Committee told me that overhead was the cost of money. I am aware that interest rates are high but I did not know that money cost 20 per cent these days. Overhead not only includes the cost of money, it includes the president's salary, the cost of the water that goes into his whiskey, the management costs and so on. The felony is now compounded by the request for money which is to be borrowed under this Bill. The Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) has indicated that he wants to give $725 million a year to the two major railroads to cover their alleged losses on transporting grain and to cover the federal Government's contribution to capital improvements. The Minister does not say what the subsidy will be for their so-called losses from hauling grain and how much it will be for capital investment. In other words, the $725 million a year provided under this borrowing Bill and the money provided under future borrowing Bills will be sent to the railroads in the form of a cheque to be spent as they please. I know that the Minister talks about guarantees of railway performance, but he has already had for Some years all the authority he needs under the National Transportation Act, the Railway Act and the Canadian Pacific Railway Act to require that performance under the law. Additional so-called guarantees are superfluous at best.
No private enterprise, bank, or lending institution would provide investment capital without getting some kind of assurance of return on that investment. How much longer will successive Liberal and Tory Governments put up funds for capital investment on behalf of the people of Canada and include in those public funds what amounts to almost a 40 per cent profit? While I am not against a reasonable profit, I challenge anyone to tell me that a 40 per cent profit is reasonable. No self-respecting free enterpriser would suggest that. He would probably say it was exorbitant.
We have an alternative use for the money that has been proposed by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin). We suggest that out of that $930 million per year, $380 million would go directly to the railroads to pay the real shortfall between the statutory grain rates and their actual out-ofpocket costs. We would not add 21 per cent return on investment on those subsidies for the benefit of the railways, or 20 per cent more for so-called overhead. They would be reimbursed for the actual out-of-pocket costs which include maintenance, depreciation, wages and salaries and fuel. The remaining $550 million is for capital investment. Assuming that it is divided equally between CN and CP, the Government's equity ownership on behalf of the people of Canada and Canadian National automatically increases by that amount, which I believe is a $ 1,000 per equity ownership share.
Of the money that is being turned over to Canadian Pacific for capital investment purposes, which is being borrowed on behalf of the people of Canada, not one nickel or return is available to the people of Canada on that investment. Surely that is some kind of economic stupidity. Surely it makes sound economic business sense to take equity ownership in return for whatever we give to each railway. Any interest or dividends that are paid year after year would come back as a return on that investment to the Government for the people of Canada.
Borrowing Authority
That type of practice should be expected of any operation, whether private or public. In approximately 50 years' time the return on that investment makes that debt not a Government expense or a total dead weight on the people of Canada but an investment which self liquidates. In fact, there may even be an odd occasion when a profit is made on the investment as well as an annual return. I do not understand how any so-called private enterprise Government-and they have been doing it in the country for 117 years-can fail to at least blush when it continues to borrow money for capital investment purposes for which there is not even an opportunity for a return on the investment.
I am just an innocent stubble-jumping prairie boy. I do not pretend to know the ins and outs of high finance, economics and so forth, but I still cannot get it through my head what kind of economic sense there is in what the Government is trying to promote. What kind of rationale is there in borrowing money to give to someone else for a capital expenditure and receiving no return on the investment? I do not understand it.
If these birds over here or the ones over there had done that with their own money, they would all be on welfare. They rise and complain about the big deficit, the poor taxpayer and the national debt, but who has been borrowing money since 1867? Who has been handing out billions of dollars in the last 117 years for capital projects, both publicly and privately-owned, with no provision for a return on those investments? Who has been doing that?
It was not any socialist. It was the Grits and Tories, the great free enterprisers or protectors of property! Whose property? The taxpayers of Canada borrow the money. It was given to someone else for capital improvements, which meant property. Do the taxpayers of Canada have any interest in or return on the property? No, the property belongs to somebody else. What about the property rights of taxpayers for the funds they borrowed and gave to Canadian Pacific for capital investment on which they will receive no return? They have no say in the expenditure of those moneys. They have no shares, no dividends or no interest. What kind of economic stupidity is that? What kind of a con game is that on the taxpayers of Canada, and also in this instance on the grain producers of western Canada?
For the same amount of money the Minister of Transport proposes to expend, we would increase equity ownership in Canadian National. We would also start taking common share equity voting stock ownership in Canadian Pacific Limited in order to have some dividends and interest in return for the investment. Surely that is the proper way to expend the borrowings any Government of any political stripe has to make frequently, in fact every fiscal year.
Concerning the matter of capital investment to improve our rail systems in western Canada, although everything in and east of Manitoba, had been left out, the Minister said that for

May 5, 1983
Borrowing Authority
anything over 31.5 million tonnes a year the farmers will pay all the freight costs. When he was asked yesterday whether he would lift the ceiling, he said that if farmers shipped 41.5 million tonnes, it would cost the federal Government $1 billion more. He said that he could not do that, that he could not lift the ceiling. But, he is prepared to allow it to cost grain producers by 1991 $1 billion a year more. He borrows this money, on which there is no return, to hand it out, and then passes the cost back to grain producers and taxpayers generally. I hope we will have some answers. We want to know why this insane economic spending has been going on and for what purpose the borrowings will be used.

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1983-84 (NO. 2) MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Bill C-151, An Act to provide supplementary borrowing authority, seeks to borrow an additional $14.7 billion. Of this amount, $2 billion may be carried over into future years. The Government is thus seeking a cushion of $2 billion for this year plus $2 billion to be used either this year or in future years. It is more than a cushion. It sounds as if they were looking for the whole chesterfield.
The Government has come to Parliament seven times in this session to seek more borrowing authority. We have had Bills C-30, C-59, C-lll, C-125, C-128, C-143 and C-151. This clearly indicates that the Government has not paid any attention to the Auditor General's statement that the Government has no control over expenditures. The Auditor General went to great lengths on the problem of the borrowings by the 300 or 400 Crown corporations that we have. There is absolutely no accountability from Crown corporations. I will go into that in a little more detail in a moment.
The Government's projected financial requirements between 1983-1984 and 1986-87 total $93 billion. Parliament is in for a steady stream of large borrowing Bills over the next few years. It clearly indicates that the Liberal Party's solution to any problem is to spend more and borrow more.
Financial requirements are only part of the picture. Many Crown corporations are able to raise debt in the financial markets without seeking borrowing authority from Parliament. That is something we in the Conservative Party oppose. When we were in Government, we took steps to bring in some control. Unfortunately this was dropped when the Liberals were returned to office.
I now want to deal with the federal Government's financing in perspective. There will be Government project spending of $100.1 billion on a national accounts basis and a deficit of $31.3 billion on a public accounts basis. The gross national debt last March was about $160 billion. Interest on the debt will cost Canadian taxpayers $17.6 billion this year. On a per capita basis, Government spending this year will amount to $4,000 per man, woman and child in Canada. This compares to only $500 per capita in 1967-68.
The cost of interest on public debt this year will equal $700 per capita and $1,800 per taxpayer. That is a tremendous load on the Canadian public. One tax dollar in three is used to service the debt.
In the Fall of 1979, Treasury Board found that it was faced with cost over-runs on major capital projects totalling $1.1
Borrowing Authority
billion. Placed in perspective, these over-runs could finance the construction of 18 CN towers or 66 new fighter aircraft. This has been going on for years. There are cost over-runs on practically every project in which the Government gets involved. No cost benefit analysis is conducted and there are no proper controls on these projects.
Including operating deficits and capital expenditures, Mirabel airport to date has cost the taxpayers more than $700 million. This was to build an airport that was way ahead of its time, was not required and was aptly named a white elephant. That sum of money is the equivalent of giving 800,000 people a free round-trip ticket from Saint John's Newfoundland to Vancouver, British Columbia.
The federal Government has an information and advertising budget of $245 million. It does not need any such budget. Most of this advertising is an absolute waste. In 1981, the federal Government spent $13.1 million on food, booze and entertainment. That is the equivalent of more than one million bottles of liquor. Since this Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) came into office in 1968 he has been repeating the same thing every couple of years. They are empty, meaningless statements. I will quote what he has said in the past.
The Liberal Government has a history of paying lip service to restraint. In August, 1969, in announcing the first Liberal restraint program, the Prime Minister told Canadians that, "We would be on the road to financial disaster if nothing was done to bring spending under control". Why does he not do something about it? This Government should do something about that. In June, 1975, in announcing the second Liberal restraint program, the then Finance Minister told Canadians, "The Government proposes to set an example of restraint ... by imposing strict control over its activities and programs".
In spite of periodic references to restraint, Government spending has climbed by 554 per cent on a public accounts basis since 1968. Any commitment on the part of the Liberal Government to restraint, based on past evidence, is nothing more than insincere posturing.
We in Manitoba get the double whammy. We have the same problem with the NDP Government there. Because of the NDP budget deficit and uncontrolled spending, the Manitoba financial rating has dropped. Manitoba's financial position has deteriorated significantly over the last two years, a major New York ratings house suggested yesterday as it lowered the Province's credit rating. The Province has budgeted for an equally large deficit this year. Government spending will increase by almost 10 per cent this year after adjusting for inflation. The credit rating has been downgraded because of excessive spending and excessive borrowing. Manitoba, under an NDP Government, has one of the largest debts in Canada. In 1969 we had a balanced budget. The Conservative Government was defeated in 1969 and the NDP took over. Prior to 1969 there were proper financial controls. Once the NDP got in, uncontrolled spending began. That is why Manitoba is in this mess today.

May 5, 1983
Borrowing Authority
Over the past 15 years, Government spending has risen in an unprecedented way. On a national accounts basis where data is comparable over time, spending has climbed from $12.6 billion in 1968-69 to an estimated $100.2 billion in 1983-84, an increase of 693 per cent. On the more commonly used public accounts basis, spending has increased from $12.3 billion in 1968-69 to $89.8 billion, an increase of 554 per cent. That is astronomical and insane. A significant portion of the increase has happened since re-election of the Liberals in Feburary, 1980. Relative to fiscal 1979-80, spending has risen by 78 per cent on a public accounts basis or 84 per cent on a national accounts basis. Spending this year will go up by 12 per cent. Why will spending go up by 12 per cent? It should not be going up at all. Spending on a national accounts basis is now equal to 26 per cent of Canada's Gross National Product. This compares to 21 per cent only four years ago. In 1982, borrowing by the federal Government accounted for 51 per cent of all net new security issues placed in Canada. Borrowing of that magnitude must clearly have an effect on the supply and demand for money and thus on the interest rates that must be borne by the private sector. The horror stories go on, Mr. Speaker.
The investment community does not trust a Government that continues to live so far beyond its means. It does not want to hold a currency that continues to be debased by excessive Government borrowing. As a consequence, the dollar has fallen, driving up the cost of living in Canada. Interest rates remain quite high as the Government attempts to support the dollar. Job-creating capital investment has gone elsewhere. A classic example of that was the National Energy Program which almost destroyed the Canadian oil industry, lost some 60,000 jobs in Canada and drove oil rigs out of the country. jThe Government stijl does not get the message. The mqd spending goes on. The mad borrowing continues. It does not learn from its past errors and mistakes. It just carries on with the same ridiculous procedure.
I mentioned earlier that there is no proper accounting by Crown corporations. They are simply handed money and, as the Auditor General says, they take the money and run. I want to read the following passage from the Auditor General's Report of 1982:
It may be helpful in visualizing the scale of the problem to think of the whole group as an enormous iceberg floating lazily in the foggy Atlantic; silent, majestic, awesome. The public tends to see only the upper portions ... the giants like CNR, Petro-Can, CBC ... The great bulk of the iceberg below the surface is less spectacular, less likely to attract public interest, less likely to receive the attention of Parliament, yet costly to taxpayers.
Of course, the Auditor General's Reports have read the same every year for many, many years. It is unfortunate that more attention is not paid to their recommendations.
Dealing with entrenchment of state control, the creation of the multi-billion dollar holding company, the Canada Development Investment Corporation-not to be confused with Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation-belies any serious commitment the Liberals may profess to have regarding greater accountability for Crown corporations. The CDIC was
created in May, 1982, by Order in Council. Six months and 17 Orders in Council later, the CDIC has emerged as a huge holding company for Government corporate interests with no accountability to Parliament and a wide open mandate to intervene anywhere in the Canadian economy. One of the first things the present Prime Minister did when he took office in 1968 was to remove parliamentary control over Government expenditures. Any politician who plays games that do away with proper accountability or control over the public purse is a very irresponsible individual.
The new corporation has been granted a $500,000 interest-free loan from the Consolidated Revenue Fund, and the Minister responsible, Senator Austin, claims that he can commandeer the profits from Teleglobe, which now go to the CRF, and use them as a source of operating funds for the CDIC. That is a great accounting procedure, Mr. Speaker.
Canadair has hit the headlines recently. It will be looking to Parliament for about $2.5 billion to bail it out. In December of 1976,1 told the Liberal Government that it should-
-quit hiding behind the cloak of secrecy-
-and make a complete revelation of all details with regard to Canadair, the Government-owned aircraft manufacturing company, including the $50 million loan guaranteed by the Government. I was concerned than about the $50 million. That has gone up to the $2.5 billion that they are looking for now. Back in 1976,1 pointed out that:
-Canadair has to sell 500 aircraft just to recover the investment let alone cost of money over the intervening period . .. The Gulfstream Two which is the obvious competitor to this aircraft has established a strong position in the market but sales are well below the 200 level.
In light of those figures, I pointed out:
Where is the Canadair Ltd. going to find the market for 500 aircraft?
, That) question ljst still relevant tqday. Are we to continue to prop up Canadair? When they come to us looking for this $2.5 billion, we will have to Find out if they have a market or if they have sales for 500 aircraft. They will probably have to sell 1,000 aircraft to break even now. But at that time, the Minister, who is the present Energy Minister (Mr. Chretien) and was the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce at that time, always gave us great assurances that there would be no problem with Canadair, and he ridiculed me and my colleagues for even bothering to raise the question. We warned them in 1976 that they were on a disaster course, but they laughed at us. Now the laugh is on the Canadian taxpayer.
Canadian people are quite concerned about a recent speech made by the Secretary of State (Mr. Joyal) in which he points out that he is going to turn Canada into a French state. In his speech he points out that the cost will be no object. No one is to question the cost of turning Canada into a French state. He goes into a fair amount of detail in his speech but we do not know how much it will cost, we do not know what effect it will have on English-speaking Canadians, and we should be entitled to have a White Paper or a Green Paper or some kind of an explanation from the Government on how much it intends to spend on turning Canada into a French state.
May 5, 1983

The Minister in his speech talks about the need for more French universities across the country. I do not know how many more are needed, what the cost will be, where the money will come from, where they will be located. Our universities at present are all suffering from the current economic conditions. They can hardly keep going. But this Minister says that he will build more universities across the country. It would be very interesting to know if any cost benefit analysis has been done in regard to turning Canada into a French state.
Another cause of considerable concern across the country is the fantastic cost of the language training programs to date. About $4 billion has been spent on language training. The majority of Canadians will go along with a reasonable amount of language training at a reasonable expenditure, but $4 billion just for language training is only a very small part of the total cost of making Canada a fully bilingual country.
The double standards used by the Liberal Government in its language training program is of concern to us. Certain people, friends of the Government, will be sent to the south of France for language training. Other individuals from the Government are sent to Toronto for language training and have apartments rented for them. One recent case was brought to light where an individual was sent to Toronto to learn the French language. The Government rented her an apartment for $845 a month, gave her an expense account of $600 a month, plus her salary while she was in Toronto for 11 months. I have other contacts here in Ottawa, Mr. Speaker, individuals who have had difficulties learning the French language. The Government will not give them language training in the Government schools and they will have to go to night school and pay for their own language training.
I could go on and on about the fantastic costs of the Metric Commission and their extravagant expenditures and how their budget has risen 100 per cent this year to a grand total of over $25 million. I would suggest that the Government should start reading the Auditor General's report, never mind coming back here every couple of months to borrow billions and billions of dollars more.
