speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I regret very much that I am compelled to make the remarks I am about to make. I have to say as a Member of Parliament of Canada that I have been betrayed. It cannot be described in any less forceful term than that.
When I first became a Member of the House of Commons in the Fall of 1972 I was concerned about the fact that we were embarked upon a bilingual program. I wanted to know what was to be the impact upon my constituency in particular and upon Canadians in general. I was asked to attend a meeting with the then Member for Moncton, the then Member for Saint John, the then Member for Fundy-Royal and the then Member and still Member for York-Sunbury (Mr. Borrowing Authority
Howie). We met with Mr. Spicer who was then the gentleman in charge of the bilingual program for this nation. We asked several questions. First, how was it determined that a particular position in the Public Service would be classified as bilingual? It was not exactly a fair question at that time and Mr. Spcier could not directly answer it. I then asked whether he could tell me that unilingual communities would be categorized as those requiring bilingual employees in the federal service. The answer was an unqualified no. My next question was, if there was a competition for a particular job within the Public Service of Canada, will language prohibit the employment of any person applying for public work? The answer was: no, because there would be language training provided. If the applicant were approved and if additional language training were required it would be available to the gentleman or the lady who applied for the job before employment. Another question asked was: would language have anything to do with advancement in the service of those already employed? The answer was, no. The policy of the Government was that if there is to be advancement and if bilingualism were a requirement for advancement, then language training shall be available.
It was not very long until the government welshed on the first statement that language training would, in fact, be available for an applicant who had the merits to take the job for which he had applied. The first step and the qualification of Mr. Spicer's statement was that the individual would have to take an aptitude test. If the person failed to pass that aptitude test there would be no language training. Regardless of merit, if the individual did not have the aptitude for bilingualism, he or she shall not get an appointment. That was a very serious move away from the formula outlined by Mr. Spicer.
The next step now in place is that you must be bilingual to apply for some jobs and you will not get one if you are not. The language resolution of 1973 followed that. Again, we were assured the guidelines that had been outlined to us by Mr. Spicer would, in fact, remain in place under that resolution. That, of course, had been practised up to that point in time to a degree that I was quite satisfied the resolution did not infringe upon any statements made to me as a new Member of Parliament by Mr. Spicer. I was the idiot who then betrayed myself and my constituents. I voted for that resolution, and for that I apologize to Canadians, whether they live in St. Andre or St. Stephen, Fredericton or Edmundston. I do not care what their principal language is, people are entitled to opportunity for public employment. They should in no circumstances be denied employment regardless of their native or mother tongue. That is an injustice to any person young or old who applies for a job in a professedly bilingual country.
When it comes to advancement, I do not have time in the 20 minutes allocated to me to enumerate the denials of language training for those who applied. I do not have time to list the extravagances of some of those who did get language training and the cost incurred, but I am concerned that in the Town of St. Stephen there are now three National Revenue postings

Borrowing Authority
which may or may not have been filled and which are declared bilingual. Only one is available to a unilingual individual. I am ashamed that I voted for that resolution. One of the applicants for those National Revenue jobs went to see the RCMP. He assumed he was talking to a personnel officer and he was told by that officer that if he was not bilingual he should not bother to apply. I challenge anyone here in his House or anyone who reads my statement to say that I am against a bilingual program in this nation of Canada. But I say that bilingualism has to be for all Canadians. Employment has to be open to all Canadians whether they come from St. Andre or St. Stephen. That makes no difference to me, but the language training has to be there and the merit system has to be in place. People in this nation have a right, which I thought was extended and explained in 1973, to apply and expect to be accepted for employment regardless of language qualifications.
When this is carried to the extreme, we see instances of people who are already in the employ of the Government of Canada, most of whom are over 50 years of age and some of whom are over 60 years of age, employed by the Department of Transport for security purposes in the City of Fredericton at the city airport who are advised they shall be released from their job four months down the road because they are not bilingual. That is why I feel I was betrayed and they are betrayed by this Government.
There is no example in the annals of this nation of more obvious betrayal. Why is it that there are now several research positions in the field of agriculture left vacant? Have they been declared bilingual? I could not care less what the mother tongue of an individual is so long as he can study the research projects and come up with the merits that qualify him for employment. I could not care less. But he has to be good, and it should not be language that should categorize him.
I appeal to this Government to come back to the promise it made, first through a very highly respected gentleman, Mr. Spicer, and second through a resolution that was passed by this House, one for which I voted, and for that I apologize to all Canadians, not just those in my constituency. That promise was with regard to the pattern of bilingualism intended, and that is the pattern which I can support. I cannot support the automatic disqualification for linguistic capability on its own. I cannot support the lack of opportunity for advancement for linguistic reasons alone. Train the people and advance the people if the merit is there. That is the system we must have.
It was rather interesting to listen to the last speaker from the New Democratic Party. If a fellow were going to finance this country on the basis that he proposed, you would have to get the Canada goose to lay golden eggs. It sounded to me as though he had about as much economic sense as a computerized, vocalized teddy bear.
There are a lot of items on which I would like to expand with respect to the borrowing Bill, with respect to the. budget and with respect to Canadians as a whole. Amongst those things I am going to ask a question or give notice of a question to which I hope we will get an answer in this debate, the budget debate, or in some form. The proposed changes in the Crow rate structure which pertain primarily, superficially at
May 5, 1983
least, to the West, also have economic impact on the East. We never did get an explanation of the impact on the East. We never did get an evaluation of the increment in cost which would accrue to the feeders in eastern Canada, and particularly to the feeders east of Montreal and including all of the Atlantic Provinces. There is an impact and I want to know if there is any intention on the part of this Government to recognize that increment in cost which will be passed on by the change in the Crow rate as it relates to eastern Canadian poultry, hog and beef operations. We are entitled to that answer in a definitive cost study basis, Mr. Speaker. Let us have it because we cannot assess it since we do not even have the legislation or the firm proposition. Maybe the press has, but this House does not.
We are prepared in this House for a request to vote for a borrowing Bill, the consequences of which are shameful in this nation, as far as I am concerned, but it does pose some questions. You and I, Mr. Speaker, happen to be representing constituencies which need some money. We need some money from this make-work salvage operation which is coming up in the potato industry, and we need it very badly. One could extend that further if one went farther down the river westward into Quebec from my home, eastward into Nova Scotia. We need some money in the apple industry. The apple industry is facing the results of what I consider to be an error, although I am not overly critical of this. It is the root stock evaluation for climatic purposes. The apple industry in eastern Canada planted a root they never should have planted, and grafted onto trees which were supposed to bring profit, and which have not turned out to be. I submit to you, Mr. Speaker, that that root should have been evaluated in the climatic conditions in which it was planted. It never was evaluated. It was released for production. It was sold and it was multiplied in this country. Unfortunately, we now have some apple growers who have lost up to 50 per cent of their total orchard as a result of replanting with a root stock which would not stand the climatic conditions of our country.
The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) said, "Well, if anyone would declare it a disaster, we would do something about it. If the Provinces would put up a little money, we would do something about it". However, Mr. Speaker, that has been a historical federal responsibility, and anyone who suggests that it is not a disaster when crop damage as high as 50 per cent takes place in any aspect of agricultural operations is wrong. That, Sir, is disastrous.
However, the real disaster at the moment is in the potato industry. It has always been cyclical ever since that crop was first planted in a commercial way in Atlantic Canada or, for that matter, in any other part of Canada. Its returns have been so variable that some people have said that you might just as well shake dice as plant potatoes. And to some degree that is correct, with all the variables which exist. But this time we got hit with both barrels. We got hit by weather which caused the crop, first, not to store well and, second, even if it stored, to be
May 5, 1983

graded so that it became virtually unmarketable. The return in your constituency, Mr. Speaker, and mine, dropped down to as low as 15 per cent or 20 per cent of the cost of production of the crop.
There are several steps which the federal Government should take. I propose that it should move now. I would ask the help of any sympathetic Hon. Members on the Government side of the House to encourage Government to act now. The cropping season is just around the corner. The steps which the federal Government should take are, first, to put some of this make-work money, some of this pump-priming money, into the Farm Credit Corporation to be lent at reasonable rates to those farmers who need assistance; second, to defer the payment of the money which has been lent for the storable crops program. That would enable some farmers to plant a new crop. Third, and this is the last step which I would recommend, the Government should sit down with the provincial Governments and in fact come up with a program which is supportive of both the apple industry and the potato industry. But it must do it now because now is the time to plant. This is the week of decision, and if that decision is not reached, if there is not cooperation between federal Government, provincial Government, farm organization and banks-and they are all ready to talk-if that decision is not reached by next week, Mr. Speaker, you and I know that there will be people who should have help who cannot plant another crop.
I appeal to the people of responsibility, Mr. Speaker: you have less than a week to make that decision! I am not talking entirely about young farmers who have over-financed or overborrowed. I am talking about farmers of every age in the business, from farmers with less than ten years of experience to farmers with more than 40 years of being self-supporting in the agricultural field and producing that crop. They are all dependent upon the degree of damage from mother nature, in storage, excessive moisture and distortion of the tubers. Every category of farmer in this instance is in very, very serious trouble. I cannot over-emphasize the need and the urgency of an immediate decision.
There is another place for some pump-priming money. Some of that could be put into make-work projects in the coastal region of my constituency. I have submitted on an annual basis, except for this year-it seemed to be an exercise in futility; the list must still be on file and nothing has been done about it-a list of port improvements, small craft harbour improvements. I have submitted up to 30 names, some of which have never even been inspected by the Department of Public Works. It is not their fault. There was no use inspecting them because the Department of Fisheries did not give them any money, and this is the time when money could and should be spent either for a dual purpose or for a single purpose, whatever the case may be. It would be for a dual purpose in the Town of St. Andrews, where a proper harbour facility for fishing and tourism would add a great deal to the economy of that community. The same could be said for St. George. It could be spent in the Sand Point wharf where it was promised
Borrowing Authority
three years ago that if the tuna packing plant in that community would triple its capabilities, the Government of Canada would in fact extend the wharf to accommodate the necessary ships to bring products in and take other New Brunswick products out. That has not come through yet, Mr. Speaker, and that wharf is cluttered up. We are losing business. Canadian workers could be at work but now they are going to East Port, Winter Port and other ports along the main coast. We are losing business because the Government has not kept its word. And it is not just the tuna packing plant. There are products being shipped from the Atlantic coast of this continent which will not go through Saint John or Chatham or Rimouski, but would in fact go through Sand Point Port in Champlain Industrial Park in Charlotte County.
There is a place where some of that money could be put, and not only will it make work but it will make continuing work and bring on-going revenue to those communities. I could read the list of small craft harbours ad infinitum. Dipper Harbour, they are: Chocolate Cove, Whale Cove, Seal Cove, Ingalls Head. These harbours have been neglected. Let us put some of this money to work to make work where it will have lasting and productive value. These are the things, I believe, Mr. Speaker, which we have to consider. That would be a constructive allocation of make-work money.
There are other projects in the Province of New Brunswick which deserve attention as well, many others, but the ones referred to are the ones which would be revenue-producing and work-producing for the long term. Money could also be spent on tourist development throughout the whole Province of New Brunswick. The provincial parks could be improved, which would increase their attractiveness. That is a place where money could be put. Some of the highways could be improved, country highways, in order to attract tourists to this Province, to make it an all-season operation.
I must, Mr. Speaker, say to this House, to my constituents and to Canadians, that I have been betrayed in the bilingual program. I supported it. I have to ask that it revert to what it was. Canadians have been betrayed and their resources mismanaged. When I go home on Mother's Day and look at our family, my children and grandchildren, I tell you that I will not be going with the pride with which I would have gone 20 years ago. They had a future then in a country of which the then campaigning Prime Minister could say "this land is strong". Well, Mr. Speaker, this Government sure sapped its strength.

speakeroldname: Mr. Andre Maltais (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce and Minister of Regional Economic Expansion):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1983-84 (NO. 2) MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to be taking part in the debate today, especially after listening to the comments of the Member for Carleton-Charlotte (Mr. McCain) which of course concerned the entire question of borrowing authority for the Canadian Government. I think the Member for Carleton-Charlotte had some very interesting

May 5, 1983
Borrowing Authority
things to say about the importance of carrying out certain projects in his riding, where funds could be put to good and practical use, because basically, I think he shares the concerns of Members on both sides of the House, who are anxious to ensure that the money the Canadian Government gets from private or corporate citizens or by borrowing will generate jobs and stimulate the economy. However, I disagree when the Hon. Member says that we do not have the same pride we had fifteen years ago, because there is less of a future for young people. I think it is true that the situation is a difficult one today, but I think it is wrong to conclude that there is less future in this country than there was fifteen years ago, because if we look at this country's potential and compare it with other industrialized countries, it is clear that Canada's position is still very strong, although a great deal more effort must be put into building and modernizing our infrastructures.
I think the Member for Carleton-Charlotte-whom I know very well since we travelled together when I was vice-chairman of the Transport Committee-and you yourself, Mr. Speaker, as an Eastern Canadian, are both aware of what it means to lack infrastructures of every kind in our ridings, especially in our part of the country.
I think the Bill we are considering today, Mr. Speaker, namely Bill C-151, an Act to provide borrowing authority so that the Government may, according to the wording of the Bill, invest such sums of money as may be required for public works and general purposes, mean a great deal to us. All this may not be as important to Members from urban areas, because they are used to living, I should perhaps not say in luxury but in relative comfort; many good roads, industry nearby and a highly diversified economy. If we look at the extra-peripheral regions, however, there is an incredible lack of infrastructures. I myself am from an area that is not necessarily remote but nevertheless suffers from the problems of regional disparity and has done so for quite some time. At first, 1 was opposed to a Government deficit. Like all Canadians, we would prefer a budget in which revenue and expenditures are balanced. That is not the case, unfortunately. Because of the present recession and the problems in industry, the Government's revenue has been much lower than was predicted by the experts and by the Government itself, so that while funds must be spent on social benefits for Canadians, Government revenue has dropped considerably. If the Government had ignored what had to be done in this country, perhaps we could have had a balanced budget, but this would have been at a high cost to the extra-peripheral regions and Canadian workers.
I am thinking of the Gaspe, which is just across from my riding. Mr. Speaker, it is high time the Canadian Government announced substantial measures to improve infrastructures in that region. A lot has been done in the Gaspe over the last fifteen years, but this region will never be able to operate on an equal footing with the rest of Canada if we do not give it the necessary capital facilities so that it will not only be able to
compete with other parts of Canada but also with other countries. This is important, and I know what I am talking about, Mr. Speaker.
Similarly, I think a person has to know the Atlantic Region to realize that Newfoundland, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island have far fewer infrastructures than they do out West, and I am referring to the Pacific Region. A person has to have seen both to understand the significance of the funds being sought by the Government today for investing in those regions. If it were just a matter of spending money on facilities that are already more than adequate, I would object.
Earlier, however, the Member for Carleton-Charlotte was very specific when he mentioned the particular needs of his riding. I think the same applies to most ridings in the Atlantic Region.
All Members from Eastern Canada have very specific needs as far as infrastructures are concerned. As long as we do not have proper infrastructures in that part of the country, we shall never be on an equal footing with the rest of Canada.
That is the important thing. To be able, with a budget like the one we have now and the supplementary funds that must be ratified, to invest in capital projects. And I have often heard some of my fellow Canadians criticizing the Government because according to them, it was putting the country into debt. But although it is true, I think people should realize that in doing so, we are rescheduling projects which would otherwise have been carried out five, ten or fifteen years later.
However, the projects that will be financed in 1983-84 will serve future generations. These infrastructures will last ten, fifteen, twenty, twenty-five or forty years. It stands to reason therefore that the cost be spread over one, two or three generations.
Last week the Minister of Transport of Canada (Mr. Pepin) came to my riding to announce that Ports Canada will finally build new infrastructures in the Bay of Sept-Iles. People have been waiting for those facilities for years, but the work was supposed to be spread over 15 years. Thanks to the combined efforts of various intermediary groups in the area, and thanks as well to the unrelenting work of people responsible for regional communities, the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Transport gave their approval to this harbour project.
We have already asked the local people to get involved and make sure that private businesses will be able to open their doors in the Sept-Iles area so that the facilities in the port of Sept-Iles will be more productive. After the announcement was made last Thursday, Mr. Speaker, we could see that the outlook was changing already. Contrary to the comments the Hon. Member made earlier to the effect that the people-the young, the elderly, heads of families and retired people alike- were desperate, they now have regained confidence. They are glad that they will finally be able to find work and, as a result of the mining problems we have experienced, we must diversify
May 5, 1983

our regional economy. It must be done. And very soon the Government will have to open up a transportation link between Quebec City and Port-Cartier, which has been closed since 1979.
If I wanted to be irresponsible, Mr. Speaker, I would say that it was closed down when the Progressive Conservative Party was in office. However, that Party did not have anything to do with it, such was the economic situation. Since 1979, Quebec and the Government of Canada have appointed very responsible people to look into the possibility of reopening the plant at Port-Cartier. That is when we will need funds to guarantee a sound recovery, not as owners of the plant-in that respect, I think I am voicing concerns similar to those of the Progressive Conservative Members-not to become owners, but to act as partners in the reopening of that plant.
Indeed, we had done our share in 1974 through the allocation of funds for the Port-Cartier plant to make sure that the area would have a truly diversified economy. The funds for which we are seeking the approval of the House will be used for that kind of operations. I still remember when I was Deputy Chairman of the Committee on Transport; we had toured the Atlantic region and I recall the dilapidated condition of wharves and fishing facilities. I remember that some wharves had been abandoned altogether although fishermen did need them to do their job. The funds will therefore be used to carry out various projects in those ridings and those areas.
Mr. Speaker, the budget was not introduced only to benefit the party in office; it is aimed at all Canadians and all ridings. I think that the role of the Opposition is to make sure that everybody gets his share and that the real needs are met. That is the important thing to say at this stage. I would suggest that all Members on both sides of the House are aware of the importance of this budget for young people.
To criticize the legislation introduced in the House is easy but what really matters is to know what are the needs this budget is going to meet, and these needs can only be met if the money necessary to carry out these projects is made available to us. What surprises me is the fact that over the past two years, Hon. Members both on the government and opposition sides have repeatedly urged the Government to take positive action in an effort to get the economy moving again.
Yet, Mr. Speaker, the Government is acting responsibly. Not only does it provide $2.5 billion for direct job creation, but it urges the private sector to get involved by providing it with some $4.5 billion in incentives and tax breaks of all sorts.
I think it is most important to let Hon. Members and all the other Canadians know that this is a concerted effort by both the private and public sectors to balance the forces, because the Government has no money. What the Government has is the taxpayers' money. That is all the Government has, and it can only rely on human and natural resources, and seek a
Borrowing Authority
perfect balance between these two resources to develop the country. That is all it can do. As a Government, we cannot create the economy, but we can and should create favourable conditions to a buoyant economy. That is what a Government must do. And that is exactly what the budget introduced by the Minister of Finance is trying to achieve. Because there are no miracles, Mr. Speaker, only concerted efforts in the right direction.
Already Hon. Members opposite are blaming the Government for the borrowing powers it is seeking. Had we not borrowed money or introduced legislation which was bound to increase the deficit, would we have had the tools to break the economic deadlock? I believe the answer is a very definite no, Mr. Speaker.
When you read the comments made by various economic experts, you very soon realize that the budget does meet current needs. Of course, there may be some reservations here and there. We could have allowed a little more here, a little less there, but all in all we struck a balance. And this is what the Government should be striving for, in the interest of all Canadians. On the lower North Shore of the St. Lawrence River, Mr. Speaker, there lies an area with some 400 miles of coastline where there are no roads, absolutely none, although 6,000 or 7,000 people do live there, in 15 isolated villages, French-speaking, English-speaking, and native people. Those people are looking forward to a reorganization of both Regionair and Quebecair. I think the Minister of Transport should be urged to act soon. For instance, Mr. Speaker, those people have to pay $700 for a round trip ticket from Blanc-Sablon to Montreal, and that is not first class. There are many stopovers, although this is the same country and the same Province. That is not normal. Special steps will have to be taken, at the Canadian taxpayer's expense, so those people can travel from Blanc-Sablon to Montreal at a more reasonable cost. Right now, it is cheaper for a Montrealer to go to Paris than for someone in Blanc-Sablon to go to Montreal. Those people have a right to live, and they have made tremendous efforts to provide Canadians with fish, and game.
But, when we speak in this House, we have a feeling we are speaking only to Torontonians, Montrealers, Vancouverites. This country is not just ten provincial capitals and one federal capital, Mr. Speaker. It consists of a vast land with a potential that is waiting to be tapped and in need of infrastructures. This has often been neglected in the past, for all sorts of reasons. But past neglect is no reason for staying on the same course. Quite the opposite! As a Member of Parliament, I wish we only had balanced budgets. But in the face of unbelievable shortcomings that exist in various parts of the country, whether it is the East, the Centre, the West or the North, I feel we really should invest with a view to the future, and get the money needed to have the required infrastructures.
Our young people are asking for two things, Mr. Speaker, two very specific things: a sound training, and infrastructures

May 5, 1983
Borrowing Authority
that will enable them to put their training to practical use, to develop this country. This is what our young people are asking for. And older people too. We know all about layoffs in the various mining operations across the land. This involves not only Shefferville, Gagnon, Fermont, Port-Cartier and Sept-lles, but many other communities. When we see people put on early retirement at age 50, 55 or 58, it is a real tragedy. A person who receives a $10,000 severance pay is not necessarily happy. The only way to be happy is often to have a job that you like, a job that makes you proud to support your family, to be responsible for them, to be a responsible citizen. That is what people need.
I remember how frantically the officials from the Department of Finance wanted to check the outflow of money in order to try and lower the deficit. However, when one is elected to sit in this House, one realizes the real needs of people and one has to say no to public officials' demands in order to be really responsible and allocate funds in an attempt to put people back to work and help industrialize this country. That is what we really need. We sometime hear the question: How is it that the government does not plan ahead for such expenditures? I remind Hon. Members that when the IOC mining company shuts down its operations in Shefferville, the Canadian government-that is to say each of us-will pay $4,500 per household to relocate the people of Shefferville anywhere else in Canada, even though they cannot find a job, because people cannot stay up there, they cannot stay in a remote place 385 miles North of Sept-Iles, where there is no road, when a return plane ticket between Shefferville and Montreal costs in excess of $350. So it is up to the Canadian government, to the public administration, to take on the responsibility of enabling people to relocate elsewhere in order to look for a brighter future. The mining company will pay $1,500 and the Quebec government will also put up $1,500. Yet, this was not anticipated in the government budget. And these people from Shefferville, who were paying a lot of taxes, are quite justified to expect the government to help them find better prospects elsewhere.
So for all these reasons, I suggest the bill we introduced is necessary, and in conclusion, because my time is expired, I would ask Hon. Members on all sides of this House to show extreme care in distributing the funds in all parts of this country, to ensure that each and every constituency will have its share to invest in the future of our country, among young as well as older Canadians, so that every Canadian can regain hope not only in the future of this country, but in themselves, because the great crisis we are presently going through is in great part a crisis of self-confidence. So I will simply say in concluding my remarks, Mr. Speaker, that I hope we will gain the support of all parties so that this bill can be passed as soon as possible and that tomorrow, we will be confident that, the country is back on track and heading toward prosperity and a more diversified economy.
A motion to adjourn the House under Standing Order 45 deemed to have been moved.

subtopic: FISHERIES-NEGOTIATIONS ON RESTRUCTURING EAST COAST INDUSTRY. (B) NEWFOUNDLAND PROPOSAL

speakeroldname: Hon. James A. McGrath (St. John's East):
subtopic: FISHERIES-NEGOTIATIONS ON RESTRUCTURING EAST COAST INDUSTRY. (B) NEWFOUNDLAND PROPOSAL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on May 2 I put a question to the Minister of State for Economic Development (Mr. Johnston) who is now in charge of the Cabinet committee which is charged with the responsibility of restructuring the Atlantic Provinces' fishing industry and the troubled companies in that industry. I wanted the Minister to tell the House when the negotiations leading up to a decision on restructuring would be completed and when a decision would be made and reported to the House.
Of course, I got no satisfaction from the Minister. That is why I am taking this opportunity to bring it to the attention of the House. This is a very serious matter.
On March 28, a conference was held in St. John's with all the principal players involved in the Newfoundland fishing industry. A resolution was unanimously adopted and forwarded to the Minister of State for Economic Development. I will read it into the record:
BE IT RESOLVED:
That all fish plants involved in the deepsea fishery be kept open, and BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED:
That the federal and provincial Governments make a commitment to exercise their separate jurisdictions in the harvesting and processing sectors to ensure the continued operation of all deepsea ports, and BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED:
That rather than a simple bail-out of the corporate interests both Governments commit themselves, jointly or separately, to the public ownership-in whole or in part-of those deepsea companies unable to operate without public assistance, and

subtopic: BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED.

speechtext:
That the immediate acquisition of these companies, either jointly or separately, by both Governments is absolutely necessary to accomplish a meaningful restructuring of the Fishing industry, and BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED:
That the option of the separation of the fleet and community ownership of processing plants be examined as potential objectives in a new, restructured deepsea fishing industry.
That resolution was unanimously adopted at this conference and was signed by Members of Parliament, including the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans, the Hon. Member for Humber-Port au Port-St. Barbe (Mr. Tobin), the Minister of Fisheries of Newfoundland, the Minister of Environment of Newfoundland, the President of the Newfoundland Fish Food and Allied Workers Union, the President of the Newfoundland Federation of Labour and the mayors of all the towns affected by down plants. To date there has been no response from the Government to that resolution.
May 5, 1983

We are dealing with a situation in which there are still seven plants in Newfoundland not operating. Thousands of inshore fishermen have no place to sell their fish and trawler fleets are tied up. This situation exists a full six months after the Kirby Task Force Report during which time negotiations on restructuring were supposed to be taking place.
The Canadian Salt Fish Corporation is still without a president, even though the Government accepted Kirby's recommendation for an expanded role for the corporation which would see it involved in processing and marketing fish in the northern communities of Newfoundland and Labrador.
The Fisheries Council of Canada has just completed its annual meeting in St. John's, yet there is still no word from the Government on restructuring, in spite of an ongoing negotiation, we are told at least, by the Government Cabinet Committee and Kirby.
What we are seeing here is the Newfoundland fishing industry being relegated to a secondary role to that of Nova Scotia which, if the Cabinet committee has its way on restructuring, will see a newly integrated giant Nova Scotia corporation as the principal player in harvesting, processing and marketing of fish in the Atlantic Provinces.
My question is, where is the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans for Canada (Mr. De Bane) while life and death decisions are being made affecting Newfoundland communities, fishermen, plant workers, trawler men and their families? I am talking about thousands of people. His role has been usurped by one of the super Ministers of the Cabinet, the Minister of State for Economic Development, a gentleman who obviously takes his advice from the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. MacEachen) who is an active Member of that committee and happens to be the Hon. Member for Cape Breton-Highlands-Canso. Of course, there is not doubt as to where the interests of that hon. gentleman lie.
I say to the House that our patience is running out. There is unanimity in Newfoundland as to what should be taking place, yet the Government in the interests of protecting certain corporate interests insists upon dragging its feet. The innocent pawns in all this are Newfoundland fishermen-14,000 inshore fishermen, thousands of plant workers who are without jobs, trawlermen and their families. They are the innocent pawns in this super corporate power chess game which is taking place.
I say to the Government that our patience is not infinite. Time is running out. I call upon the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans, who signed his name to the resolution which represented a reasonable compromised solution that would address the problems of the Newfoundland fishing industry, of the downed plants and of the communities that see their livelihood taken away, to rise in his place and tell us when we can expect a decision by the Government. At the very least he should tell us when we can expect a reply to the resolution which was forwarded to the Government on March
Adjournment Debate
29. To this date there has not even been the courtesy of an acknowledgement.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jean Lapierre (Parliamentary Secretary to Deputy Prime Minister and Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Minister responsible for economic and regional development, as chairman of the ad hoc Committee of Ministers on Atlantic Fisheries Restructuring, has the over-all responsibility for the ongoing negotiations on restructuring. We know that the Hon. Member is impatient; so are we. On March 31 the Government gave Michael Kirby broad instructions to begin negotiations leading to a reorganization and refinancing of the troubled deep sea fishing industry in Canada. Mr. Kirby is representing the Government in those negotiations. These ongoing negotiations with the banks, the companies and the Provinces concerned are presently at a very delicate stage. I know the Hon. Member would not want those negotiations to break off because of some indiscretion or an attempt to make political points.
All Hon. Members will understand that we are dealing with matters of utmost financial sensitivity and that any details relating to the Government's negotiating position cannot be laid before the House at this time. The Hon. Member will know exactly what we have done whenever the negotiations are concluded. However, I am confident that these negotiations are proceeding on an urgent basis-and the Hon. Member has shown the urgency of the case-and will lead to the revitalization of the Atlantic fishing industry, including the provision of more stable employment and incomes for thousands of fishermen and plant workers who depend upon the fishery.

subtopic: INCOME TAX-AUDITING OF FARMERS' INCOME-REQUEST FOR MORATORIUM. (B) REQUEST FOR LIMITATION ON ASSESSMENT OF BACK TAXES
INCOME TAX-AUDITING OF FARMERS' INCOME-REQUEST FOR MORATORIUM. (B) REQUEST FOR LIMITATION ON ASSESSMENT OF BACK TAXES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the subject I want to raise this evening concerns Section 31 of the Income Tax Act. I think Hon. Members on both sides of the House who have farmers in their constituencies realize the problems that are caused by the interpretation of Section 31. Most of us, especially myself, are having problems because the Department of National Revenue is very actively engaged in auditing farmers across the country under the provisions of that Section.
What has happened is that because of tough times, high interest rates and high costs, many farmers have been required to work off their farms to make supplementary income to keep up with their payments and literally to keep from losing their farms. To add insult to injury, the Department has picked this particular time to audit farmers and to reclassify them under Section 31.
Section 31 has roughly three classes of farmers having regard to writing off losses against income. There are bona fide farmers who farm full time. They are allowed to write off as much loss as they have. The second category of farmers includes those with supplementary income. They are allowed to write off $5,000 per year. Then there is the so-called hobby

May 5, 1983
Adjournment Debate
farmer classification. We are not interested in protecting hobby farmers.
What is happening is that because people have had to work off their farms in order to make supplementary income, they are being categorized as hobby farmers. This causes an awful lot of difficulty. People are finding that their losses are being disallowed and that they are now being hammered with as much as four years in back taxes, plus interest and penalties. In many cases they are literally being forced to either sell their farms, stock, equipment or whatever they can to try to pay their tax bills.
Literally hundreds of farmers in my riding, have been audited. Let me read a paragraph from a letter I received today from the Quesnel and District Chamber of Commerce. Quesnel is a community in my riding of about 10,000. The letter is addressed to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde). The first paragraph points out the problem. I quote the last paragraph:
The farmers in our community are afraid to commit present financial resources to such things as fertilizer and seed badly needed at this time of the year while under the threat of possible income tax reassessments for prior years.
In my question on April 26,1 asked whether, because of the ambiguity of Section 31 and the reclassification of many of these farmers, he would call a moratorium on tax audits until Section 31 could be amended to reflect these problems. This problem has been with us since 1951 when the section was brought in. I did not get an answer to the question. My second question was:
Would the Minister agree to that, to assess back taxes only for the current year if people are going to be reassessed under Section 31.
There is a precedent for that. This problem arose in 1972. The then Minister of National Revenue, now President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Gray), wrote to the former Member for Mission-Port Moody. I quote from that letter:
If, following the review, it is concluded that the departmental policy has been correctly applied to a taxpayer, I have asked that this allowance of losses be limited to the most current of the years under review. This basis of assessment will be continued in all subsequent applications of the departmental policy relating to losses claimed by part-time farmers so that only the loss for the one year is disallowed.
Under the circumstances, that precedent should hold. The least we can do for farmers faced with this terrible problem is allow their losses for the current year.

speakeroldname: Mr. Garnet M. Bloomfield (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Revenue):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Revenue
subtopic: INCOME TAX-AUDITING OF FARMERS' INCOME-REQUEST FOR MORATORIUM. (B) REQUEST FOR LIMITATION ON ASSESSMENT OF BACK TAXES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member has raised a number of questions on the subject of audits conducted by National Revenue concerning claims for farm losses. The Minister has answered all those questions. For the benefit of the Hon. Member let me explain the interpretation and application of the law with respect to this matter.
Section 31 of the Income Tax Act sets a limit, under certain conditions, to the amount of losses from a farming business that a taxpayer may deduct from other sources of income in completing a tax return. The word "business" here is of crucial
importance. The taxpayer must be in the business of farming in order to claim business losses, a reasonable requirement.
The Hon. Member has asked for a moratorium on tax audits because he says the section is ambiguous. Although the section is somewhat complex, the Department has the benefit of many court decisions, including one by the Supreme Court of Canada to which it can refer for interpretation and application of the law.
The Hon. Member has also commented on the qualification of the auditors performing the audit. In this regard I would like to say that the Department's auditors have the know-how to determine the profit or loss of an enterprise. For example, if an enterprise incurs thousands of dollars of expenses in a year and in the same year makes only a few hundred dollars in sales and does this for three or four years in a row, and it can be seen to be making no progress toward a profitable position and the entrepreneur is really living on money earned in another full-time job, the question must arise as to whether the enterprise is a business at all. This would be true whether we are talking about agriculture or any other type of business.
The Member suggested that the reassessment of taxes should only be for one year. The Department recognizes that it can take more than one year to get a person established on a farm. I am sure the Hon. Member would understand that in many cases it takes a few years to assess the viability of an enterprise. Therefore, in these circumstance^ it is normal, depending on the facts of each case, that the Department may review and assess, where applicable, for more than one year.

subtopic: NUCLEAR ARMAMENTS-U.S. AND U.S.S.R. OFFERS TO REDUCE NUCLEAR ARSENALS. (B) PROPOSAL TO HOLD SUMMIT MEETING
NUCLEAR ARMAMENTS-U.S. AND U.S.S.R. OFFERS TO REDUCE NUCLEAR ARSENALS. (B) PROPOSAL TO HOLD SUMMIT MEETING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when I questioned the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) yesterday on the nuclear arms negotiations issue I tried to make the point that Canada should play a stronger role for peace in the world by pressing both the Soviet Union and the United States to make progress in Geneva. By pressing, I mean that Canada should be formulating its own recommendations to both super powers for mutual, balanced and verifiable reduction in nuclear arms, and that these recommendations would be based on objective account of the precise amount of nuclear weaponry that the Warsaw Pact and NATO possess.
At one level the nuclear arms question is terribly complex, yet it is possible to ask clear questions to which clear answer should be given. Here are some of the questions a growing number of Canadians, including Parliamentarians in this House, are asking. Exactly how many warheads does each side have? Why are the two sets of nuclear negotiations, strategic and intermediate, not joined into one over-all negotiation so that the question of nuclear parity can be established? Why does the Security Council of the United Nations not play a major role in the negotiations?
I submit that there is an important role for Canada to play in pressing forward in this manner. Nuclear negotiations are
May 5, 1983

not a matter in the exclusive domain of the two super powers. All humanity is today held hostage by the arms race.
It is the growing recognition that the nuclear arms race must be halted that led two important bodies in the United States to take action this week. The U.S. House of Representatives, by a margin of 278 to 149, passed a resolution calling for a mutual and verifiable nuclear weapons freeze. This vote has not only given the nuclear freeze movement credibility, but renewed momentum. The congressmen did not take this action lightly. They debated the resolution a total of 45 hours, with several amendments being made. Consider the debating time on that crucial issue compared with what the Canadian Parliament gives this issue in debating time-practically zero.
The Roman Catholic Bishops of the United States, by a vote of 238 to nine, ratified a broad-ranging pastoral letter that denounces nuclear war and calls for the end of nuclear weapons. The Bishops, in calling for this immediate halt, have taken a forceful and historic position in church thinking and put their collective finger on the nub of the issue by saying, and 1 quote from The New York Times of May 4, 1983:
"The nuclear age is an era of moral as well as physical danger," ... "We are the first generation since Genesis with the power to virtually destroy God's creation. We cannot remain silent in the face of such danger."
No one can accuse the American congressmen or Bishops of being soft on communism or of being dupes of the peace movement which is growing rapidly around the world. Both the House of Representatives and the church in the same week have urgently signalled that negotiations must be successful if mankind is to survive.
A clear, solid path to common security is found in the Palme Report signed by representatives of the Soviet Union, the United States and several other countries including the Third World. This report called for a zone in central Europe to be cleared of battlefield nuclear weapons. My colleague, the Member for Victoria (Mr. McKinnon), pointed out in a lengthy analysis of the Palme Report that the report:
-came up with recommendations that are practical and feasible. There is a way out of this mess and I think that the Palme Commission has shown us that way.
Let the Prime Minister and the Canadian Government become more vigorous in pressing for the detailed recommendations of the Palme Report, in pressing the Security Council to play a role in unified negotiations and, finally in pressing for a summit meeting of the two leaders, Messrs. Reagan and Andropov, who hold the future of humanity in their hands.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jean Lapierre (Parliamentary Secretary to Deputy Prime Minister and Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: NUCLEAR ARMAMENTS-U.S. AND U.S.S.R. OFFERS TO REDUCE NUCLEAR ARSENALS. (B) PROPOSAL TO HOLD SUMMIT MEETING
speechtext:
Adjournment Debate
My hon. colleague has suggested one way of resolving the nuclear escalation and if we were to follow his arguments and manage to get together the partners who, for instance ... He says that some clear and specific questions should be asked in order to get clear and specific answers. I would therefore ask him to consider the discussions that were held on this issue during the past years and to realize that when we refer to equal and equivalent nuclear forces as between Americans and Russians, various interpretations are given. Moreover, this issue is so confused that it would be difficult for us as good Canadians or as citizens of the world to simply ask the Russians and Americans to draw up an inventory of their weapons and those of other countries. I think that one is rather naive and fails to realize what is going on when one asks that sort of questions.
On the other hand, for the past few years, the Canadian Government has been strongly promoting the resumption of negotiations, especially as regards the Geneva talks.
We have also noted the many contacts made by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacEachen) and by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) himself when the Hon. Member refers to the possibility of a summit meeting, as the Prime Minister has confirmed yesterday that during his meetings with President Reagan and Vice-President Bush he urged the American authorities to agree to meet their Russian counterparts at a summit conference. Moreover, we should make sure that if such a summit meeting were held, it would be well prepared in order to give concrete results. An agenda for a summit meeting of that sort should not be forced upon us, and I think that Canadians generally agree that it is essential that such a meeting be convened. In addition, the Prime Minister and the Government are making serious efforts to get that kind of activities under way. However, we hope that there could be a summit meeting similar to the one which was held in 1972, that is when the Salt I Agreement was signed. We hope that perhaps in the future another similar exercise could be carried out with the complete agreement of the entire world which is anxiously waiting for a respite in the nuclear arms race.
